#2727. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2724. Will the NFC North Teams All Win 10 Games?

In NFL history, no division has ever seen a last-place team win 10 games. It sort of almost happened in the NFC North last year, as the Green Bay Packers, Minnesota Vikings and Detroit Lions all finished with 9 wins, and in 2023 the Cincinnati Bengals finished last at 9-8 (and had several chances to get to 10), but that's kind of it for close calls. Prior to 2002, the NFL had 5-team divisions, and so this was functionally impossible. And since the league went to a 17-game season in 2021, it is much more likely now.

The four teams of the 2026 NFC North are all quite good, and all have at least six wins as we enter week 10. No team is perfect, but the Lions have an outstanding offense, and their defense has improved with some players like safety Brian Branch getting healthy. The Vikings have a truly elite defense and have now re-added quarterback Kirk Cousins for the stretch run. The Bears and Packers have both been quite good on both sides of the ball, with the Packers slowly fixing their offensive line, and the Bears adding defensive lineman Jeffrey Simmons to help shore up their defense. These teams will all continue to win games.

In short, there's a great chance that this division winds up with every team at 10-7 or better. I put together a very, very simple projection for the rest of the season (I want to stress how simple this was; it's ugly, in Excel, and I made it primarily to work through what happens based on who wins the remaining division games, because I kept messing this up), and every team finishes with 10 wins in 30% of simulations. Every team finishes with 11 in almost 5%! (Yes, it is mathematically possible for every team to finish with 12, but it's extremely unlikely.)

Weird hypothetical projections you made while Outlook was down are one thing, so let's try to be more concrete. The Bears have seven wins in the bag, and while they have some very tough games against Buffalo and Jacksonville, they also get the Saints and Dolphins, which almost surely gets them to nine. They would then need just a single division game (of their four remaining, two against Detroit, one each against Minny and the Packers) to get it done.

The Vikings have six in the bag, with games remaining against the Commanders, Jets, Falcons, and Panthers. That might get them to ten without any additional help, but they also have three division games left, one against each North team, in addition to a tough battle with the 49ers.

The Lions also have six in the bag with non-division games against the Giants, Titans, Falcons, Bucs, and Patriots, teams that range from "meh" to "atrocious. Even if they fail to win four of those, they still have the Bears twice, and the Vikings and Packers each once.

And our Green Bay Packers, who sit at six wins, get the Rams without receivers Davante Adams or Puka Nacua, the Saints, the Dolphins, and the Texans, in addition to a tough matchup with the Bills. They will also face the Vikings in Kirk Cousins' first game back, and one more each with the Bears and Lions.

When you look at it like this, you can really see how the ten-win scenario is really pretty likely, and how the eleven-win scenario is downright plausible. Even in this analysis, I focused primarily on the out-of-division games. Remember, someone HAS to win the in-division games, too; they are not just hypothetical. Let's take a look at a fairly negative scenario for the Packers as an example.

Let's assume the Bears and Lions split their remaining division games, each going 2-2, with the Vikings going 2-1, and the Packers finishing 1-2 in their remaining division games. That means, before accounting for any of the aforementioned trash out-of-division games, the Bears are 9-4, the Lions are 8-5, the Vikings are 8-3, and the Packers are 7-5. This puts the Packers in the worst spot, but still needing just three wins between New Orleans, Miami, Houston, an undermanned Rams team and Buffalo. It's pretty likely! And in the event the Bears drop an additional division game or two, bolstering the Packers/Lions/Vikings, remember they have a one-game lead.

So, unless the division falls apart, this is VERY likely to happen. The Packers have the misfortune to play in one of the best divisions in the history of football. And I, for one, cannot wait to travel to the 7-10 NFC South champions for the first round of the playoffs.

#2723. 2026-27 NBA Minutes Report: Injuries to Lauri Markkanen, Stephen Curry impact Western Conference landscape

Welcome to the NBA Minutes Report. He will be out for the next month at least, and I detailed the fallout in a video I recorded on Monday. Brandon Miller is also dealing with a groin injury, and Dennis Schroder has a hamstring strain, so the Hornets are not in the best shape right now.

Caleb Wilson suffered a hand injury on Wednesday and only played 15 minutes. It remains to be seen how long that might keep him sidelined. That would likely mean more usage for Matas Buzelis and Josh Giddey. Norman Powell is also dealing with a shoulder injury, and his name has been mentioned in trade rumors already, so the Bulls seem unlikely to play him until he's fully healed. That said, Chicago did get Nic Claxton back, and his minutes should continue to tick up over the next few weeks at the expense of Jalen Smith.

The core of the Cavs rotation remains unchanged, but Sam Merrill is out with an elbow injury, which has led to more minutes for Meleek Thomas and Tyrese Proctor. Thomas looked good against the Knicks on Wednesday, and it would not be a surprise if he continued to play himself into a larger role.

Santi Aldama returned in the last week, which led to some minutes hits for all the big men, including P.J. Washington and Daniel Gafford. That part of the rotation could get more crowded when Dereck Lively II (foot) returns as well. Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving continue to pace this offense, and I recorded a video about how good Flagg has been this season.

The Nuggets run a tight rotation, and not much has changed since last week. DeMar DeRozan is seeing his minutes trend down a bit as the core group gets more usage and Spencer Jones returned from his injury. DeRozan figures to be just an ancillary piece on this team, barring injury.

The Pistons are another team with a narrow and consistent rotation. Isaiah Joe and Jalen Duren both remain sidelined, but Duren has begun on-court activities, so he could return from his hamstring injury in 2-3 weeks.

Obviously the big news for the Warriors is last night's injury to Stephen Curry, which I wrote about on the website today. With Gary Payton II also out, Brandon Williams suffering a hamstring injury, and both Moses Moody and Jimmy Butler recovering from knee surgeries, the Warriors are very short-handed. We should expect to see a bump in minutes for De'Anthony Melton.

With Steven Adams and Clint Capela sidelined by injuries, the Rockets may have the narrowest rotation in the league. It seems that both players could return this weekend, so we'll see what that does to the frontcourt minutes in Houston.

With Tyrese Haliburton (hamstring) still sidelined for another two weeks, the Pacers are relying a lot on Andrew Nembhard and Aaron Nesmith. The issue is that Nesmith left Wednesday's game with knee soreness and did not return. If he were to miss time, Kelly Oubre Jr. would figure to step into a larger role.

We might be getting closer to seeing Brandon Ingram take the court for the Clippers, but that time has not yet come. That leaves the Clippers in a precarious situation. Brook Lopez's return has meant fewer minutes for Isaiah Jackson, and Derrick Jones Jr. has been playing big minutes alongside Darius Garland. There's not a lot to get excited about here.

Walker Kessler has been a tremendous addition to the Lakers, and I covered his success in a video this week. He's the clear third option behind Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves, and the rest of the team is ancillary pieces. Reaves did have X-rays on his heel, which came back negative, but he could still miss some time. Collin Sexton also had to get stitches in his forehead on Wednesday, so he may miss a game or two as that heals. If both Reaves and Sexton are out, that would lead to a bigger role for Quentin Grimes.

Things are status quo from Memphis right now. Javon Small has moved into a role in the rotation, which has impacted the minutes for Cedric Coward, and Isaiah Stewart sat out for two games earlier in the week. It's possible that Kris Murray has just been phased out of the rotation.

The Heat have a very narrow rotation, and there is little to be excited about except for consistent minutes for Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo. Bobby Portis Jr. has seen his minutes trend down, and Andrew Wiggins doesn't seem likely to supplant Pelle Larsson from the starting lineup. Klay Thompson is playing a lot of minutes, but he's not the same player he was a few years ago.

I mentioned last week that Kel'el Ware and Ryan Rollins were getting far fewer minutes than I expected, and that has continued. I see no reason why the Bucks will change things up now, even if they should. Brayden Burries has been stepping into a bigger role in the starting lineup and is delivering, which I discussed in a video this week.

As the Timberwolves adjust to life without both Anthony Edwards and Donte DiVincenzo, they have given more minutes to Trey Lyles and Jaylen Clark. Terrance Shannon Jr. also missed a couple of games over the weekend but returned earlier this week. The Timberwolves are going to play their starting five for as many minutes as they can every night.

The Pelicans have a deep rotation but none of it is that exciting. Dejounte Murray returned from his brief absence, but Jeremiah Fears continues to play a much larger role in this offense. Jordan Poole is now back and in the mix, but Bennedict Mathurin suffered a thumb sprain and could miss some time.

The big story in New York is that Landry Shamet has seemingly supplanted Mikal Bridges in the rotation. Bridges will start and play minutes early, but he has seen very little time on the court in the second half and played just 17 minutes in each of the last two games. Deuce McBride and Tyler Kolek are also seeing more minutes as Bridges' role shrinks for the time being until he can get back on track. Josh Hart missed two games earlier in the week but returned on Wednesday.

We know how many injuries the Thunder are dealing with, but they got some reinforcements by trading for last year's Kings first-round pick Nique Clifford. Clifford figures to play just 15-20 minutes a game for the Thunder, but that is a locked-in part of the rotation. It's also a valuable role with Ajay Mitchell now dealing with a sprained ankle. Aday Mara has stepped into a bigger role without Chet Holmgren and looked really good in his rookie season.

The Magic continue to be one of the most injury-plagued teams. After dealing with injuries to Jalen Suggs and Paolo Banchero, the Magic now have Tristan da Silva out with a calf injury. That should lead to more minutes for Jase Richardson in the short term, but the usage will fall to Franz Wagner and Anthony Black.

We knew these 76ers would battle some injuries during the season, and it's starting now. LeBron James is out on Thursday with a back injury, and Joel Embiid could miss this game with a foot injury. None of those figure to be major injuries, but with Dominick Barlow also still sidelined, it makes the 76ers just a little bit thinner than they'd like to be.

Should the Suns play Collin Gillespie more? Yes, they need a true point guard. Will they? No, it doesn't seem like they will. Ryan Dunn has seen his minutes tick up, but this is an offense without a true floor general, and the results have been what you'd expect.

With Ja Morant and Shaedon Sharpe sidelined, we've seen an uptick in minutes for Chris Youngblood. However, Youngblood missed Wednesday's game, which led to increased minutes for Damian Lillard and Jrue Holiday. The Trail Blazers would rather not have to consistently play both of those veterans over 30 minutes per game.

Keegan Murray returned from his ankle injury and is right back to his normal role in the offense. Precious Achiuwa left Tuesday's game with a leg injury, but Dylan Cardwell was taking a lot of his minutes before that happened as well. Cardwell played 29 minutes in that game and should see his minutes totals rise because of his rebounding prowess.

The Spurs are relatively healthy and very good. Devin Vassell is out with an adductor injury, and Tobias Harris remains sidelined with a calf injury, but both of them could suit up by the end of the week. The rest is status quo,

Collin Murray-Boyles missed one game earlier this week, but he has played a bigger role with Kawhi Leonard sidelined and Scott Barnes also out with a groin injury. Alijah Martin has played more as a result of Barnes' injury, but it's not expected to sideline Barnes for too long.

The Jazz just lost Lauri Markkanen to a fractured hand after already losing Jaren Jackson Jr. to a knee injury. With Jusuk Nurkic also out with a toe injury, the Jazz are going to rely heavily on Darryn Peterson, Ace Bailey, and Keyonte George over the next few weeks. Jaxson Hayes also played 30 minutes in the first game without Markkanen, so expect that to continue.

With Justin Champagnie sidelined, the Wizards are running a bit of a shorter rotation. It's the same key names, and we should assume little will change if not for injury. Anthony Davis missed two games last week, which allowed Alex Sarr and Will Riley to play more minutes, but Davis has been great when he's on the court.

#2722. USC men's basketball defeats Cal 77-65, improves to 3-0

After opening the season 2-0, the USC men's basketball team traveled to Cal for its first true road game of the year Wednesday night. The matchup offered the Trojans an opportunity to test themselves on the road early in the season against a former Pac-12 foe.

Following a somewhat sloppy start to the game, the Trojans eventually made it clear that they were simply the better team. When the final buzzer sounded, USC had a 77-65 victory and a 3-0 start to the year.

Perhaps the most notable statistic from the game was that the Trojans had 53 rebounds to Cal's 36. Jacob Cofie—who played all 40 minutes—had 11 of those rebounds, while also contributing 15 points and six assists. Meanwhile, Alijah Arenas and Rodney Rice led USC in scoring with 19 and 18 points, respectively.

The Trojans will now return home for three consecutive games at Galen Center. The first of those will be on Sunday against Arkansas-Pine Bluff, with tipoff set for 4:00 p.m. Pacific time on Big Ten Plus.

#2721. Is there a quick fix to the Las Vegas Raiders’ defensive woes?

Immediately after his football team lost to the San Francisco 49ers 38-17 this past Sunday, Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak was naturally asked about potential changes to a defense that's now given up 30 or more points in six straight games.

"We will look at the film, and we will make our decisions when we have cooler heads," the rookie head coach said combating the need to make any rash decisions.

Cooler heads prevailed and on Monday, Kubiak expressed confidence in his chosen rookie defensive coordinator Rob Leonard and emphatically shut the door on any changes in that regard.

"No, I don't. In fact, I see us doing the things we said we were going to do better. Stand behind Rob (Leonard). Stand behind our defensive staff. Stand behind our players," Kubiak said during his Monday media availability. "And I think the world wants someone's head on a platter every time things don't go right. But the way that I see it is that we brought people here for a reason, to get a job done and develop players for the long haul, and that's where we're going."

Kubiak's decision to stand behind Leonard, the defensive staff, and the players on that side of the ball likely draws mixed feelings from Raider Nation.

After all, Las Vegas tied a modern-era NFL record of six-straight games allowing 30 or more points and team is ranked dead-last out of the 32 teams in: Points allowed (268), yards allowed (3,469), rushing yards yielded (1,361), and first downs given up (208).

Being the caboose in the league in those categories isn't a recipe for success, it's a blueprint in ineptitude.

Which beckons a question: Is there a quick fix to the Silver & Black's defensive woes?

Even if Kubiak decided to part ways with Leonard nine games into his initial tenure as an NFL defensive coordinator, the underlying issues remain — no matter who is promoted to interim play caller status. The cauldron of misery is a mix of both schematic and roster issues and it continues to simmer in a piping hot boil. There's a glaring lack of talent — particularly in the trenches at defensive tackle — and no matter what play calls Leonard deploys to make up for that — more man coverage and blitzing — the results are there for everyone to see.

The Raiders are gashed by the run and are habitually beaten through the air. Now it isn't all bad. Leonard's group showed sharper execution and focus in the second half in both Weeks 8 and 9 by rising to the occasion against the New York Jets and the San Francisco 49ers this past Sunday.

But the moments of efficiency are too fleeting.

And this shouldn't be a surprise for folk who watched the offseason.

Yes, the Raiders are in rebuild mode. Yes, the talent gaps weren't going to be filled in one offseason. And yes, it'll take the coaching staff time to truly integrate their philosophy on a roster that's going through natural turnover during this early phase of the Kubiak era. But the expected growing pains shouldn't absolve folk of criticism — from Kubiak, Leonard, and general manager John Spytek and Co.

The ownership of a historically woeful defense is a beast of burden that multiple Raiders share.

Listening to linebacker Quay Walker above is encouraging. And it's true all 11 defenders need to be on the same page on the field — ditto for the coaches and other defenders on the sideline.

Unfortunately for the Walker — the 26-year-old free agent catch who inked a three-year, $40.5 million deal with the Raiders in the offseason — he's a culprit of not playing as one, communicating, or executing properly in a glaring play against the Niners that left running back Christian McCaffrey wide open for a walk-in touchdown pass. It was a sequence that saw both defensive tackles Tonka Hemingway and Adam Butler dropping into zone coverage, with the former the "closest" defender to CMC.

"It was. Yeah, we did not peel on the halfback," Kubiak said of the play in particular, noting that play was a situation where another player just had an execution issue. "That was not those guys' (Hemingway and Butler) job, though."

That defender is most likely Walker who should've have peeled back to cover McCaffrey instead of moving towards San Francisco quarterback Brock Purdy.

But amongst the myriad of lowlights, there were highlights from Leonard's Raiders defense in Week 9. Edge rusher Maxx Crosby dropped Purdy for his fourth sack of the season just before halftime. The play showcases what is possible when all three levels of Las Vegas defense is on point — rush, second level, and backend coverage.

As does the interception by rookie safety Treydan Stukes early in the third quarter.

Kubiak waxes poetic about the culture and standard that he's continuing to instill upon his Raiders. Former starting quarterback Kirk Cousins — who was traded to the Minnesota Vikings before the NFL trade deadline this past Tuesday for a 2027 third-round pick — helped foster the high-level of play that's expected to permeate throughout the Raiders' building.

One can argue keeping Leonard in place creates a lack of accountability as the play under the defensive coordinator falls well below what Kubiak expects from his football team.

On the other hand, Kubiak backing Leonard avoids the toxicity of canning a first-time defensive boss that's growing into the role much like the head coach who chose him. Publicly backing his much-maligned defensive play caller showcases the head coach's ability to back an assistant threw serious growing pains.

And that's what Kubiak will do through the rest of the 2026 campaign. Live with his choice and see if Leonard rises to the occasion or wilts under the pressure. We don't know what's being said behind closed doors, perhaps Leonard is on the receiving end of some harsh criticism from Kubiak that never leaves Raiders' HQ?

Leonard is given a chance to work through the schematic issues. The talent and depth limitations are an offseason item — at the earliest. Las Vegas could dig into the practice squad and elevate 2026 seventh-round pick Brandon Cleveland to the active roster at some point to see if the 6-foot-4 and 315-pound 22-year old can bolster the defensive tackle position, for instance.

But until free agency next March and the 2027 NFL Draft a month later — shoot even a full offseason where Kubiak can scour potential replacements for Leonard — true reinforcements are far beyond the horizon.

In the meantime, a focus on fundamentals with defenders being in position to make plays, execution, and the continued grind is what's there for Leonard and Kubiak. Las Vegas still ranks in the upper echelon in terms of takeaways with 14 — good for sixth best in the NFL.

And that was the difference maker last Sunday when the 49ers forced turnovers to thwart the Raiders' offensive attack.

We'll see if he can become the coach the head coach believes he can be or if he continues to fumble a golden opportunity away.

#2719. Eintracht's Kalimuendo pursuit could push Tottenham- and Juventus-linked Ebnoutalib towards January exit

Younes Ebnoutalib has been in impressive form in front of goal this season, scoring eight goals in 11 appearances for Eintracht Frankfurt so far. Despite this, the 23-year-old forward has not always been a regular starter.

Eintracht coach Adi Hütter currently favours a 4-2-3-1 formation, meaning either Ebnoutalib or Jonathan Burkardt has had to settle for a place on the bench from time to time.

At the same time, reports suggest that Eintracht Frankfurt are looking to further strengthen their attacking options in January by making another attempt to sign Nottingham Forest's Arnaud Kalimuendo, who scored six goals during a loan spell at the club in the second half of last season.

Should the Frenchman return, Ebnoutalib could fear slipping to third choice up front, potentially limiting his playing time even more and making it more difficult for him to retain his place in Jürgen Klopp's Germany squad.

Although Sport Bild reports that Eintracht are keen to extend Ebnoutalib's contract, the German publication speculates that a move for Kalimuendo could push the striker towards a January exit.

The 23-year-old has been linked with several clubs, including Juventus and Tottenham Hotspur. However, a move abroad doesn't currently appear to be an option, as Ebnoutalib would prefer to remain in the Bundesliga, according to the report.

The Houston Rockets are making their case as one of the NBA's strongest teams early in the 2026-27 season despite losing back-to-back games for the first time last week, receiving praise in the latest power rankings from ESPN and The Athletic.Houston dropped three spots to No. 5 overall in The Athletic's power rankings from No. 1 the week prior. However, a glaring weakness and possible concern is that Fred VanVleet is shooting just over 40% on field goals, which is a problem for one of your starters to be shooting so poorly. On the positive side, Fred has seemed to help solve a lot of the turnover issues from last season, as he has a 4.6 assist-to-turnover ratio.ESPN dropped Houston down to 7th from first, but praised Houston's young core, calling them "the driving force behind the successful start,". However, Houston has Kevin Durant to thank as well, since Kevin Durant gives Houston a veteran scoring option, while Alperen Şengün and Amen Thompson have continued to strengthen the Rockets' balanced roster. Marcus Smart's arrival has also provided the team with another reliable option in the backcourt. Now, factoring in the Rockets' performance on Monday, with Durant and Sengun both scoring over 20 points, but most importantly ending the losing streak, and the win over Golden State on Wednesday, Houston could climb even higher in the rankings. #2715. Jim Harbaugh says Broncos used 'loophole' to base Daiyan Henley's physical on if Chargers would take less trade compensation

Los Angeles Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh told reporters Thursday that the Daiyan Henley trade fell through after the deadline because the Denver Broncos used a "loophole" to base the linebacker's physical on whether the Chargers would take less compensation.

Henley was supposed to go to Denver, with L.A. receiving a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick in return.

That exchange was agreed upon prior to Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET deadline, but, like any trade, it was pending a physical. While the Broncos didn't provide a rationale for why the transaction wasn't finalized in their Wednesday night statement, NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported Thursday morning that what Denver viewed as a "failed" physical was the official reason for it being nixed.

Henley was on the Week 9 injury report with a shoulder issue; however, he wound up playing most of the Chargers' defensive snaps last Sunday versus the Houston Texans. Earlier this season, a knee injury limited him during Week 6 practice. But he hasn't missed a game amid the 2026 campaign.

According to Harbaugh, the calculus behind the scrapped deal wasn't as simple as dissent between two medical staffs.

"Here's what I know from talking to Joe," Harbaugh said, via Alex Insdorf of "Guilty As Charged Podcast," referencing Chargers general manager Joe Hortiz.

"The Broncos based a pass-fail on a medical grade, based on whether we would take less compensation, and we wouldn't, and we didn't. And in my opinion, it's one of those loopholes that the league should really look into because it sets a bad precedent, continues to set a bad precedent."

Harbaugh, now in his seventh season as an NFL head coach, was then asked during his Thursday news conference if it's even allowed for teams to renegotiate terms pending a physical after the deadline.

"It shouldn't be, but apparently it is," Harbaugh said. "That's why it's a loophole, and teams should not have the ability to do that.

"I mean, it's a medical grade. It's a pass-fail for a medical grade. And they told us they weren't going to pass him if it was a fourth and a fifth, which was agreed upon. They would not pass them for that. They would pass him for a fourth and a fill in the blank."

When the reporter following up inquired to confirm that the Broncos tried to downgrade the second pick in the deal — the 2028 fifth-rounder — Harbaugh said, "Correct."

Denver reportedly was granted permission to revisit the terms of the trade with L.A. after consulting with the NFL on Wednesday. The Broncos, according to a Thursday report from The Athletic, determined that their medical evaluation of the soon-to-be 27-year-old Henley didn't align with the information the Chargers put forth prior to the trade agreement.

Even though Denver failed Henley on his physical due to a knee issue, it still tried to rework the deal, per The Athletic.

This, of course, isn't the first failed physical to get in the way of an NFL trade. Famously, that was the reported explanation for why the Baltimore Ravens backed out of their seismic deal for Las Vegas Raiders star pass rusher Maxx Crosby this past offseason. The Raiders would've acquired a pair of first-round picks, had Baltimore been comfortable with Crosby's surgically repaired knee.

#2713. Buster Faulkner still believes in Florida's struggling offense

Buster Faulkner has watched Florida's high-powered offense disappear over the past two weeks, but he remains convinced there is a good football team underneath the mistakes.

The Gators have scored one touchdown during consecutive losses to Georgia and Oklahoma. Faulkner attributed the decline to different problems in each game, from missed assignments and turnovers against the Bulldogs to poor situational execution and another failure to sustain drives against the Sooners.

Faulkner also discussed Florida's unsettled quarterback situation, rebuilding Aaron Philo's confidence, the effect of the struggling running game and the explosiveness Duke Clark restored upon returning from injury.

Each game was different. Two weeks ago, a lot of missed assignments really hurt us, along with crucial turnovers early in the game that I thought we could control. Those were more mental issues that you don't like and have to clean up.

When I watched last week's tape, I thought we corrected that part. It wasn't nearly as much of an issue. I thought we strained and played hard, but it wasn't enough. This past game was really about situational mastery. We weren't good on third down. If we convert half of those, the game might be different.

Then, there was the fourth down with Eric Singleton Jr. It was a play we had worked on and were ready for. You would like to have that one back, and maybe it becomes a different game. It was a tale of two different problems each week.

The one thing about this past game is I believe the kids played extremely hard. We have to find a way to create more snaps for ourselves and remain on the field.

Tramell Jones Jr. had to abort the fake because of the pressure. The ball had to come out immediately with the edge pressure right there.

There are a couple of things about that play I won't completely explain. You would like him to set his feet and try to get the ball toward the back of the end zone, but the defenders were directly in front of him. Eric was impeded a little, too. A couple of things didn't work.

There were a few things, although I don't want to say there were warning signs that it would reach the extent we've seen during the past two weeks. You can look back at certain things and know that if we didn't correct them, we weren't going to sustain the level at which we had been playing.

But I didn't anticipate all the missed assignments occurring during one game. This past game was a lack of execution and situational football.

Early in the game, you could feel that it would feature fewer possessions. I was thinking, "We have to rein in what we're about to run." You look back and ask whether we carried too much volume into the game considering how it played out.

As I said a few weeks ago, for different reasons, we haven't reached some of the things you want to call when you're ahead of the sticks. We did that early in the season and created explosive plays. We have lacked those explosives recently. We saw that Duke can hopefully bring some of that back.

There were some signs, but not to this extent. We have a lot to clean up in a short time.

There are several factors, although I won't discuss the exact details. But I still think there's a good football team in there. There are a bunch of kids who are hurting right now.

I thought they strained and played hard. They really wanted it. Maybe they pressed a little two weeks ago, but I don't think they pressed this past week.

It's a good group and I believe in them. These guys have come to work every day and understand this will be a process. It's day by day.

Our message is that we're only worried about today. Improve every day, find something to improve and take ownership of it. We're all in this together, and it's our job to get things back on track.

That's one thing we had earlier in the season. There was a lot of continuity coming out of camp, not just at quarterback but with many players.

Then, we had injuries that derailed our ability to practice and all the other things that go into sustaining success. We've had a few hiccups, and obviously, it starts at quarterback. You would like continuity there.

We're evaluating everything both quarterbacks do. They're both young. I've said that before, and I'm not going to back down from it.

One has made only two college starts. Does he want to play better? Yeah, he wants to play better, but that's part of growing up at that position. The other has made only around seven career starts.

We have to work through that and put them in good positions to succeed. We need to help them with the players around them. All of us are involved in this process.

We haven't scored many touchdowns since the South Carolina game. You obviously want to involve those guys, but there's a lot that goes into it. It isn't as easy as turning around and handing them the ball.

We've tried to get them touches on the perimeter, but defenses have done a good job coming down and taking those away. That means you have to push the ball downfield, and several factors affect your ability to do that.

We're working every day to put those guys in the best position to succeed. That isn't going to stop.

One thing I've always said about Aaron is that he has mental toughness. Many quarterbacks have become really successful after things didn't go their way early in their careers. They succeeded because they were mentally tough, bounced back and understood that they had to make the most of every opportunity.

If the opportunity is his, it's his. Sometimes taking a step back and seeing things through a different lens after you've done it can help your development.

I'm a big believer in developing that position. Sometimes it takes time with quarterbacks. We don't like giving them time, and that's part of playing the position, but it's our job to continue coaching them.

I believe in both guys. They have bright futures, and this is part of the developmental process.

Forty-five starts compared with two is a lot. You don't realize how valuable that is.

When you've started 45 games, consider the defenses you've seen, the speed of the game, the adjustments and preparing for a new defense every week. That's very valuable.

The best quarterbacks I've coached became better when they were older because of game repetitions. There's no substitute for game experience.

We can't rush these guys into becoming something they aren't yet. We have to bring them along, develop them, believe in them and put the necessary pieces around them to succeed.

That's probably a better question for him.

I'm one of those guys who says, "Rub some dirt on it, and let's go play." I've always said the No. 1 trait for a quarterback is toughness, mentally and physically.

You have to possess it. You're going to get hit in this league and the next league. Turn on the film every Sunday, and quarterbacks are getting hit. You have to get out there and play.

The beauty is that the portal doesn't open for a while. We have three games to evaluate everything.

If I tell you something, I mean it. I believe in these quarterbacks and understand that developing the position is a process. I won't rush that process. I'm going to stand by those guys, and we're going to bring them along. It's our job to coach them.

We just discussed 45 starts. What will these guys look like when they have 25 starts? It will look considerably different. That's the reality.

We'll evaluate the quarterbacks like every other position and do what's best for the Florida Gators. We take great pride in that. I think we have a great staff that can figure this out with the players we have right now, and there's a lot of football remaining this year.

Every day matters. If these guys want to play in the NFL or pursue any other goal, they're still developing. At practice today, they have to find a way to improve.

Each player has one area we've discussed improving for the betterment of his future. I believe in that process, and you won't convince me otherwise about what it takes to get this where it needs to be.

It allows the defensive line to play the pass. When the defense knows it's a passing situation, especially with the defensive lines and great coaches we've faced, those players can pin their ears back. That isn't fun for an offensive lineman.

The statistics and result won't show it, but I thought we ran the ball better last week than the week before when we handed it off outside of situational plays. I think we had 98 rushing yards before the sacks knocked that number down.

But we had around 48 snaps, 11 third downs and two fourth downs. That leaves 35 normal-down snaps, and around eight came during the two-minute offense. We had fewer than 30 normal-down football snaps. That isn't where you want to be, and it's why we have to remain on the field on third down.

I'm in the box, so it only affects my comfort level. It won't change how we call the game.

I don't think it will be frigid like Lambeau Field. It will probably be in the 40s or high 30s. Wind has always bothered me more than cold weather.

These guys want to play in the NFL and there are many cold-weather cities. They have to be prepared to do it when they're older. What better time than this week? The weather won't be an excuse.

Yes, although it can become difficult in the play-action game because you want to run the ball to establish play-action.

But we can do a better job throwing the football, staying on schedule and using different methods. Hopefully, that's something we can do this week.

Duke brings some juice, as you saw the other night. He hits the hole downhill and hits it fast.

He caught the ball on the perimeter, and that was 100% Duke. He might have broken loose if he weren't returning from another ankle sprain.

He can impact us because he creates explosive plays. Explosive players are how you generate explosive plays, and he's one of those guys.

We're glad he's back. He has a bright future here.

How many times in recent history have the Edmonton Oilers dug themselves an early hole only to surge back toward the top of the Pacific Division standings? It doesn't look like that surge will be necessary in 2026-27.

I had serious reservations about the Mike Babcock hire -- and I still do -- but Edmonton has been mauling opponents early. The Oilers are off to a 5-0-1 start while posting a plus-11 goal differential. Each of the team's wins has come by at least two goals.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2705. Mauricio Pochettino leaving USMNT for Manchester United just months after signing new deal

FAYETTEVILLE, Ga. — Barely 100 days into his second term as U.S. coach, Mauricio Pochettino is leaving.

Barring a last-minute snag, his expected move to Manchester United will become official Friday, Yahoo Sports has learned.

An expected midday announcement in England — and early morning in the U.S. — will end a whirling week of speculation and multiparty negotiations that unfolded not so quietly while he continued overseeing U.S. preparations at the national training center near Atlanta.

Sources said Pochettino, 54, will complete his two-year tenure with the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti — Saturday in Miami and Tuesday in Cincinnati — before taking charge of a storied Premier League club off to its worst start in 40 years.

U.S. Soccer officials have not commented on the situation all week.

Pochettino is scheduled to address the media early Friday, a common practice the day before a game.

Pochettino will return to his coaching roots on the European club circuit, where he worked for Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, among others, before dipping his toes into international waters for the first time with the U.S.

Pochettino had spoken with United on three separate occasions over the years but never received the luminous job. He is expected to debut Nov. 22 at Liverpool.

His U.S. finale will mark the end of a 37-match spell featuring a World Cup campaign that galvanized the nation for several weeks over the summer before a humbling, Round-of-16 defeat to Belgium.

The breakup comes a little more than three months after he and the U.S. Soccer Federation renewed their partnership with the expectation he would guide the team for four years and reach new heights at the 2030 World Cup.

But rehiring a coach with strong ties to the European scene — aside from the jobs, he has kept homes in London and Barcelona and never lived in the U.S. — came with the risk of him departing early. Even during the year-long run-up to this year's 2026 World Cup, Pochettino was reportedly on Tottenham and AC Milan's short list.

The USSF is expected to begin its search for a replacement immediately.

Potential candidates include Nashville SC's B.J. Callaghan, an assistant on Gregg Berhalter's 2022 World Cup squad and later the interim head coach; former Belgium and Portugal boss Roberto Martinez; U.S. under-23 coach Steve Cherundolo, who was hired over the summer to prepare the 2028 Olympic team; and Pelegrino Matarazzo, a New Jersey native with extensive European credentials who is now in charge of Spain's Real Sociedad.

Pep Guardiola — the famed former coach of Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Manchester City — would be on any team's list, though he seems much more likely to land in another European job and would probably demand a salary that dwarfed Pochettino's U.S.-record $6 million.

The USSF is not in any rush. Aside from having an opening just months into a nascent World Cup cycle, the U.S. will not play again with the full squad until late March. The next major tournament is the CONCACAF Gold Cup next summer. World Cup qualifying will begin no earlier than next fall.

The pathway to Pochettino's departure began Monday with reports out of England that he had emerged as United's top choice to succeed Michael Carrick, who was on the hot seat after just 10 months at the helm.

In subsequent days, United engaged in talks with Pochettino's representatives and the USSF, which had included a $10 million release clause in the contract the sides signed after the World Cup.

Carrick was fired Thursday, clearing the way for United to complete personal terms with Pochettino and finalize the USSF's fee.

After signing his new USSF deal in August, Pochettino set out to shape the next four years by introducing a dozen young players for a sweep of four home friendlies in the September-October window — a sign he was very much in it for the long run.

However, hours after opening camp Monday ahead of the Nations League quarterfinals, his long-term plans with the U.S. turned to quickly completing the United move.

#2704. NBA suspends Rockets G Marcus Smart 3 games for throwing punch at Warriors' Charles Bassey

The NBA doesn't look kindly on players who throw punches during a game. Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart was suspended three games without pay by the NBA on Thursday after throwing a punch at Golden State Warriors center Charles Bassey during Wednesday's game.

In its statement, the league specifically says the punch made contact with Bassey's face. The suspension is set to cover Houston's games against the Utah Jazz on Friday, the Washington Wizards on Sunday and the Miami Heat on Monday.

The incident occurred in the third quarter of Houston's 115-108 win. With less than a minute to go in the quarter, Smart and Bassey appeared to exchange words on the court. Smart then threw a punch at Bassey right in front of an official.

Smart was assessed with a flagrant 2 foul and ejected from the contest. He had already exited the court by the time the officials announced the punishment.

Smart finished the game with 6 points, 2 rebounds and 1 assist.

Under NBA rules, Smart faced — at the minimum — a fine for the flagrant foul and a suspension for throwing a punch, which comes with a minimum one-game ban in the NBA rulebook:

Any player who throws a punch, whether it connects or not, has committed an unsportsmanlike act. He will be ejected following confirmation during review by instant replay and suspended for a minimum of one game.

The incident occurred after Smart and Bassey got tangled up during a rebound attempt. After the contest, Rockets coach Ime Udoka said Smart confronted Bassey after the Warriors center wrapped up Smart's elbow on the play. Bassey reportedly told Smart "what are you gonna do," leading to the attempted punch.

Bassey, meanwhile, had something to say about what he called "fake toughness" from Smart:

"He's been playing dirty the whole game," Bassey said, according to Yahoo Sports' Kelly Iko. "I don't think he was trying to play, I think he was trying to get kicked out of the game."

Smart's absence didn't hurt the Rockets too badly in the end, as the team still managed to pull off a win. It probably helped that Warriors star Stephen Curry sustained an oblique tear early in the contest, missing much of the game.

Curry is now expected to miss at least two weeks with the oblique tear.

#2700. College basketball insider reveals what must happen for Kentucky to improve

College basketball insider reveals what must happen for Kentucky to improve appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

College basketball insider Jon Rothstein believes the answer to getting on the right track for Kentucky starts with the Wildcats' backcourt.

Rothstein mentioned Zoom Diallo, Mason Williams, and Alex Wilkins as three players who could determine how far Kentucky goes this season. At least one of them needs to take a major step forward if Mark Pope's team wants to finish in the top half of the SEC and earn a quality seed in the NCAA Tournament.

"The one thing that needed to happen for Kentucky to be a team that finished in the top half of the SEC and earned a quality seed in the NCAA Tournament was that one of Kentucky's guards, Zoom Diallo, Mason Williams, or Alex Wilkins, was going to need to play at an all-caliber level," Rothstein said. "Right now, you don't see any rhythm, and you don't see any chemistry on the perimeter."

"This team and Mark Pope are built on the idea of playing seamless basketball. Like Pope did at BYU."

Kentucky is coming off an embarrassing 89-69 loss to Kansas earlier this week. The Wildcats struggled to take care of the basketball, committing 15 turnovers that led to 22 Kansas points. They also made just four of their 21 attempts from beyond the arc.

Diallo led Kentucky with 24 points, while Williams finished with four and Wilkins added eight. Diallo showed he can score against quality competition, but the Wildcats need more consistent playmaking and better chemistry from their guards.

Pope's offensive system relies on ball movement, spacing, and players making the right decisions. When the perimeter lacks rhythm, the entire offense can become stagnant. Kentucky cannot afford to have that problem continue.

The Wildcats should have an opportunity to get back on track Friday against Northern Arizona. A victory would move Kentucky to 3-1 entering next week, but beating a struggling opponent won't erase the concerns that surfaced against Kansas.

#2699. Jim Harbaugh: Broncos took advantage of a loophole the NFL should not allow

Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh is not happy with the way the Broncos backed out of a trade for Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley, or with the NFL rules that allowed them to do so.

After agreeing to trade a fourth-round pick and a fifth-round pick for Henley, the Broncos told Chargers GM Joe Hortiz they couldn't go through with it because Henley's physical revealed concerns about his knee. The Broncos were still willing to trade for Henley, but wanted to give up less. Harbaugh believes physical exams should only be to determine whether or not the player is healthy, not to renegotiate trade terms.

"What happened with the trade? Here's what I know, from talking to Joe: The Broncos based a pass-fail on a medical grade based on whether we would take less compensation, and we wouldn't and we didn't," Harbaugh said. "In my opinion it's one of those loopholes that the league should really look into, because it sets a bad precedent."

Asked if it's permitted for teams to renegotiate trades after the trade deadline, Harbaugh answered, "It shouldn't be, but apparently it is. That's why it's a loophole, and teams should not have the ability to do that."

Harbaugh said the Broncos offered to say Henley passed his physical, but only if the Chargers would take something less than the fifth-round pick the Broncos had agreed to.

"It's a medical grade. It's a pass-fail for a medical grade, and they told us they weren't going to pass him if it's a fourth and a fifth, which was agreed upon — they would not pass him for that. They would pass him for a fourth and a fill in the blank. I don't know what to call that, but that's what it is," Harbaugh said.

Harbaugh is right that the NFL has set a bad precedent. By allowing teams to renegotiate trade terms after the deadline, the NFL is incentivizing teams to engage in chicanery on physical exams to squeeze their trade partners into taking less favorable deals. The Chargers refused to budge, but the NFL rules shouldn't have put the Chargers in a position where they had to make that decision.

CHICAGO (AP) — Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson will be sidelined for four to six weeks because of a broken right hand.

#2695. Fantasy Football 2026: Week 10 preview — Start/sit and more

Welcome to Week 10. The 18-Week NFL season is at its halfway point, and the trade deadline has passed. Most fantasy leagues have five weeks left before the playoffs start. Crunch time is here.

Six teams switched to a different quarterback in Week 9. It's one week later and five more new QBs are expected in Week 10, for Arizona, Baltimore, Las Vegas, Miami, and Minnesota. Three of those newbies will be making their first-ever NFL start. These QB replacements impact players at other positions. I'll highlight that as we go. Throw in a boatload of injuries and four teams on bye, and Week 10 could be a rough one for a lot of fantasy managers.

If you have a minute, check out the current wide receiver rooms for the Rams, Cardinals, and Colts. No, those aren't made-up names you can use for phony phone calls. They're real.

Every team in the NFC North is at least three games over .500. That's only happened in a division once, at any time, in NFL history. They all have at least six wins.

2. From the penthouse to the outhouse: All four teams in the NFC South have three wins. You can't even make this stuff up at this point.

3. No division has ever put all four of its teams into the playoffs, but if the season ended today, all four NFC North teams would get berths in the NFC.

4. Favored teams went 14-1 in Week 9, with only the Patriots losing.

5. The Broncos have won 16 consecutive one-score games in the regular season – the longest streak all-time.

6. The QB with the longest active win streak as a starter is…J.J. McCarthy, with six consecutive wins dating back to last season.

7. Christian McCaffrey caught the 37th touchdown pass of his career on Sunday, moving him past Marshall Faulk for most by a running back in the Super Bowl era.

8. The Raiders have given up 30+ points in six straight games, tying an NFL record.

9. Fantasy stat #1: Ashton Jeanty's receiving line on Sunday: Five catches for negative five yards.

10. Fantasy Stat #2: Both the Bengals and Packers have two wide receivers in the Top-8 at the position on a fantasy points per game (FPPG) basis.

On to week 10. Note: NE @ DET is being played in Munich. Set those lineups early! Good news for those on the West Coast – this is the last international game of the season.

Bye Weeks: Bears, Broncos, Buccaneers, Eagles

For those who are familiar with this column, you know the drill. For everyone else: The Rides, Fades, and Sleepers is an analysis of players that I think are primed for an especially strong or poor performance, often as compared to consensus expectations. This isn't a straight-up Start/Sit exercise. As a general rule, start your studs. I'll rarely list the most obvious names at a position as "Rides" because those players are almost always expected to have strong performances. You don't need me or anyone else telling you to start Jahmyr Gibbs. While this analysis is intended for season-long play, it works for DFS formats too. Half PPR scoring and Expert Consensus Rankings (ECR) are used for the column.

Each week, I'm picking a Ride, Fade, and Sleeper of the Week. The rules: The Ride of the Week can't be a truly elite option, the Fade can't be someone who nobody is starting anyway, and the Sleeper must be an actual sleeper, from down in the rankings.

Last week, my Rides, Fades, and Sleepers did well, with a lot more hits than misses, led by Fade of the Week Zay Flowers (3.8 fantasy points). You can check my work here.

Ride of the Week: James Cook (vs. NYJ). Maybe Cook should be listed among the elite options. He's quietly had a great season, with a touchdown in every week but one, but he hasn't had that monster game yet (he hasn't topped 22 fantasy points in a week). A surprising lack of work in the passing game, and Josh Allen gobbling up rushing TDs, has held him back. Well, I think this is the week. The Bills are 8.5 point favorites, and the Jets have a generous run defense. They've allowed the tenth most FPPG and fifth most rushing yards to opposing backs, plus 11 total TDs. Cook should smash this week.

Fade of the Week: Ashton Jeanty (@SEA). Jeanty hasn't topped 10 carries or 27 rushing yards in his last five outings, and he hasn't scored more than 13.5 fantasy points since his breakout in Week 1. Receiving work has kept him afloat, and I don't know how that's going to work in Fernando Mendoza's debut, which couldn't come in a worse spot than against Seattle. If the Raiders score ten points, I'll be surprised. Their implied total is 17 and I think that's unlikely. Jeanty is a clear sit for me this week.

Sleeper of the Week: DeMario Douglas (vs. DET). Douglas has emerged as New England's top receiver amid all the injuries, and they're going to need plenty from him against the Lions. He quietly put up three Top-12 weekly finishes at his position in the last five weeks. Detroit's defense has played much better of late, but that was against Miami and Minnesota. They're still allowing the seventh most FPPG to opposing WRs. This game has the second highest Vegas total of the week (51.5). Douglas is ranked outside the Top-25 receivers this week and that's too low – he's a solid WR2 this week.

Elite options this week – Josh Allen, Drake Maye, Brock Purdy, and Joe Burrow; the analysis starts below them.

Three QBs ranked in the Top-10 this week who I think will outperform:

Dak Prescott (vs. SF). The 49ers defense is playing well this season (ninth fewest FPPG allowed to QBs), but that doesn't scare me off this pick. The 49ers' offense is elite, even with all the injuries, and the Cowboys' "defense" isn't likely to offer much resistance. Dallas is going to need to score to keep up, and Prescott should be slinging it. The Vegas total for this game is one of the highest of the season (55.5).

Trevor Lawrence (@TEN). The risk here is that he won't need to throw all that much – which happened last week against the impotent Ravens. I'll take that chance. The Titans have allowed the fourth most passing yards in the NFL and they've also yielded three rushing TDs to opposing QBs. They also traded away their most impactful player in Jeffery Simmons. I think they'll keep the game competitive for a while. Lawrence should do enough damage before the game is out of hand.

Jared Goff (@NE) has to be licking his chops after what Jordan Love did to New England's secondary. It was big play after big play, and Goff can do that too with his excellent receiving weapons. I'm sure the Patriots will play better, but Goff was frustrated by Miami and Minnesota the last two weeks and is due for one of his big games.

Three others in the Top-12 who I like to beat their projections this week: Patrick Mahomes (@ATL), Tyler Shough (vs. CAR), and Jayden Daniels (@NYG). Daniels ran for over 100 yards and two TDs in the first meeting with New York (NOTE – bad weather could be an issue).

Bryce Young (@NO) is always a tough call. He threw three TDs last week, and on the season he's the QB11. But he's been highly inconsistent, with four games with 20+ fantasy points and three with fewer than 14. I like him this week, against a mediocre (at best) New Orleans defense that's bottom-third against QBs, and in a game that should be back-and-forth with plenty of scoring. He's ranked outside the Top-12 QBs this week and I think he'll have a Top-10 finish.

Other QB2-types to consider if you need it: Drew Lock (@LV, who is allowing a ton of points and the third most FPPG to opposing QBs), Geno Smith (vs. BUF), J.J. McCarthy (vs. WAS, allowing the fourth most FPPG to opposing QBs, but again, watch the weather), and Jacoby Brissett (vs. LAC).

Jordan Love (vs. MIN) is playing out of his mind, and I wouldn't sit him unless you've got another really good QB. But Minnesota's defense is no joke, and on Monday night they held Josh Allen to a season-low 14 fantasy points. Love leads the NFL in passing yards, so this is strength on strength. The Vikings have allowed the fewest passing yards and FPPG to opposing QBs. They've also allowed a league-low five touchdown passes. Two of those were thrown by Love in Week 1, and he also threw for a season high 389 yards in that game. The Vikings sacked him four times and they'll be coming after him constantly on Sunday. This game is in Green Bay, which helps.

Kirk Cousins (@GB) played very well for the Raiders this season and comes in as the QB7 on the season. I wouldn't rush to get him in lineups this week. He's obviously familiar with the Minnesota offense but he just got there, and Green Bay's defense is playing well. They're allowing the seventh fewest FPPG to opposing QBs and have been getting a lot of pressure. Cousins is also not going to be asked to air it out all the time like he did in Vegas.

Dropping lower, here are some QB2s who fantasy managers could be considering this week, but that I'm avoiding if I can: Matthew Stafford (@ARI, he has no receivers, and the Cardinals held him in check the first time these teams met), Michael Penix, Jr. (vs. KC), Daniel Jones (vs. MIA), and Justin Herbert (@BAL).

I would not start any of the three QBs making an NFL debut.

Elite options this week – Jahmyr Gibbs, Bijan Robinson, Kenneth Walker, and Christian McCaffrey; the analysis starts below them.

Three high-end backs in smash spots this week:

Here are six Rides this week, all ranked inside the weekly Top-20: Chris Olave (vs. CAR), Jameson Williams (@NE), Parker Washington (@TEN), Zay Flowers (vs. LAC, and nobody was happier to see his team trade for a capable QB), Justin Jefferson (@GB, and OK, he was even happier than Flowers), and Rashee Rice (@ATL).

The game is at home and the Vikings are on a short week, and could be without tone-setting MLB Blake Cashman, so I'm a little less scared of the matchup. #2692. Cowboys’ DeMarvion Overshown apologizes after his sideline blunder vs. Colts

Dallas Cowboys linebacker DeMarvion Overshown has apologized after receiving an unusual 15-yard penalty during Sunday's win over the Indianapolis Colts.

Overshown was inactive for the NFL Week 9 matchup but ran onto the field to celebrate after Shemar James recovered a fourth-quarter fumble. Officials flagged Dallas for "unsportsmanlike conduct" because Overshown was not in uniform.

Speaking to reporters, Overshown explained that excitement led to his mistake. He also confirmed that he had apologized to head coach Brian Schottenheimer and his teammates.

"It was all excitement. At the end of the day, I talked to Schotty about it. I apologized about it," Overshown said. "It was definitely in the moment."

MORE: Cowboys' Stephen Jones delivers blunt response to DeMarvion Overshown's costly sideline penalty

He explained that he had encouraged the defense to celebrate more after creating turnovers. However, he recognized the timing made his actions costly.

"You can laugh at it now because we won, but in the moment, fourth quarter, tied ballgame or close ballgame, you don't want a 15-yard penalty from a guy, especially that's not even playing," Overshown said. "That's a lesson learned."

Dallas, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys linebacker DeMarvion Overshown (0) goes through a drill in Frisco, Texas. Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Overshown admitted he initially did not realize that entering the field in street clothes would result in a penalty. He said teammate Dee Winters alerted him that he could not be on the field. By then, the official had already noticed his celebration.

"That's when I looked back and I had already seen the ref, he's pointing at me," Overshown recalled.

The linebacker accepted responsibility and promised to avoid another incident. "But I learned. It won't happen again," he said.

Overshown also made clear that the incident would not change his enthusiasm for teammates making big plays.

"It's not going to change how passionate I am about my teammates when they make plays," he explained.

He even joked about how he would handle future celebrations. "In the future, I'll have my helmet and my uniform (on), so it won't be a flag."

MORE: Cowboys' Dak Prescott refuses to make 49ers game about personal revenge

Dallas eventually defeated Indianapolis 27-23, but the penalty exposed another discipline issue. The Cowboys committed 14 penalties for 153 yards during the victory.

At 4-5, Dallas needs better discipline as it prepares to face the 7-1 San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. Overshown's apology addresses his mistake, but the team's penalty problems remain a concern.

#2690. 2026 Week 10 rooting guide for Cowboys fans

The Cowboys' victory over the Colts last week, despite all of the frustrations that came with it, allowed them to keep hope alive in the NFC East and improve in the NFC wild card race. As improbable as playoff contention feels right now, the win in Indianapolis preserved enough mathematical possibilities that we'll keep looking at things with unabashed optimism.

Sitting 13th in the NFC standings before last week, Dallas rose three spots as the Buccaneers, Cardinals, and Falcons all lost and fell to 3-6. Arizona and Tampa's head-to-head wins over the Cowboys make it especially important that they stay firmly behind us.

Still, the NFC playoff scene looks pretty exclusive right now. The top five teams are easily San Francisco and the entire NFC North. Whichever teams come out of the NFC East and South are likely fodder for their eventual wild card opponents, even with home games.

That said, many fans would still love to see the Cowboys rally and make the playoffs, however brief their postseason run may be. Here's how they're currently situated in the big picture.

1. San Francisco 49ers 7-1 (4-1 vs NFC)2. Chicago Bears 7-2 (5-2)3. New York Giants 5-2-1 (3-2-1)4. Carolina Panthers 3-5 (3-3)5. Detroit Lions 6-2 (4-1)6. Minnesota Vikings 6-2 (4-1)7. Green Bay Packers 6-3 (4-3)_______________________________8. Seattle Seahawks 5-4 (2-3)9. Los Angeles Rams 5-4 (3-2)10. Dallas Cowboys 4-5 (2-4)

Unfortunately, there's little chance of Dallas building momentum this week as they host the conference-leading 49ers. Barring a total stunner, the Cowboys' probable drop to 4-6 could allow some of those 3-6 teams to creep back above them in the standings. It's only Week 10, though, so there's still ample time to rectify it.

Aside from Dallas shocking the world with an upset over the Niners, what else should Cowboys fans be rooting for this week?

The last time these two met, it ended in a tie in Washington. The rematch in New York is predicted to go the Giants' way, but it wouldn't be a huge surprise if the Commanders pull it off. Between the NFC East race and a motivational boost before their own game, Washington's success would be a beautiful thing for the Cowboys.

The Eagles are on a bye this week, putting their disastrous season on a much-needed pause.

Minnesota at Green Bay is mostly a toss-up. Both are at six wins and helping build the NFC North's wall around playoff spots. But the Packers' first-round pick makes for an easy tiebreaker, with the hope that they eventually fall out of the tournament and keep the Cowboys' likely draft position no worse than 18th.

Someone has to win the NFC South (seems like we say this every year), so it might as well be Carolina. The best thing for Dallas is that they get hot and put losses on all of their division rivals, especially Tampa Bay, to keep them off our backs.

While Arizona does have that pesky head-to-head avantage over us, the Rams are actually between us and a wild card spot right now. Los Angeles is more like to find a late-season groove, so they're the bigger threat.

Easy interconference picks this week. Detroit and Seattle are hurdles to jump in the Wild Card race, and Atlanta is right behind at 3-6. While having a vested interest in New England losing, given the seventh-round pick they owe us, a Lions loss could be more beneficial.

If you're going to pay attention to any all-AFC games this week, the Titans are the Cowboys' next opponent. Their season is already trashed at 1-7, and we'd like them to stay deflated when they head to Dallas next Sunday.

With Chicago and Tampa Bay also on byes, it's a light week for the NFC. The Cowboys are up against it with Niners, so hopefully the other Week 10 action helps to mitigate the likely damage.

#2689. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B
