#2688. Evan Mobley out Friday with toe injury

Cleveland Cavaliers power forward Evan Mobley will miss Friday night's game against the Miami Heat due to a sprained big toe, according to the team's official injury report. Mobley suffered the injury late in Wednesday's game in New York when he went up for a block and taking a hard fall.

While there is never an opportune time for an injury, losing a key piece of the front court ahead of a date with the Miami Heat will be difficult to overcome. Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo make for a very formidable front court duo, and having Mobley would have helped counter them immensely. Jarrett Allen, who recently returned from an injury of his own, will be tasked with securing the interior on defense next to Mario Hezonja or Peyton Watson.

Mobley played 33 minutes on Wednesday, finishing with 10 points, five rebounds, four assists, and one block. He shot 4-8 from the floor, but had an overall quiet stat line.

The Cavs started Tyrese Proctor for a game with Allen out, and could opt to do the same with Mobley not available. Watson, who had a very nice game defensively against the Knicks, may slide over to power forward to make room for Proctor. Jaylon Tyson, who also returned from injury, is another candidate to start. Hezonja's size may make him a more ideal candidate for additional playing time, though he had a mostly forgettable game on Wednesday.

Mobley has generally faired well on defense against Antetokounmpo, relative to the rest of the league. Giannis will still dominate games and impact winning, but Mobley has been able to use his size and quickness to at least be a deterrent. The Cavs will not have that Friday night, making it an even more daunting task to slow down Antetokounmpo and the Heat.

According to the German tabloid, Arsenal's Kai Havertz is the clear number one, with Klopp valuing the former Bayer Leverkusen attacker's intelligence, movement and experience at the highest level.

Rather surprisingly, Eintracht Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib currently sits second in the rankings. The 23-year-old made his first two appearances for Germany in September and, although he was unable to really convince, his impressive early-season form has apparently propelled him high up the pecking order.

The same applies to third-placed Niclas Füllkrug, who is on loan at Werder Bremen from West Ham. Having missed Klopp's first squad, the striker was handed a call-up this time around after climbing to the top of the Bundesliga scoring charts with nine goals.

Jonathan Burkardt, Nick Woltemade and Deniz Undav complete the hierarchy in fourth, fifth and sixth place respectively, having all missed out on the squad this time around.

Should Havertz, Ebnoutalib or Füllkrug pick up an injury, Burkardt would be first in line for a call-up as the next-ranked striker.

#2682. Brad White says Florida defense must strain with greater focus

Brad White made Florida's defense relive all 20 plays of the drive that sealed its loss to Oklahoma.

The Gators' defensive coordinator opened Monday's full-unit meeting with the possession to illustrate how individual mistakes accumulate. White said the defense did not lack effort or desire, but its players failed to combine their strain with the focus necessary to execute straightforward assignments and escape the field.

White also discussed his return to Kentucky, Ben Hanks III's growth, Myles Graham's recent play, Jayden Woods' pass-rush development and Joseph Mbatchou's expanding role.

I obviously have history there and many great relationships.

But, like anything in life, you have relationships from the past; keep up with them and wish those people the best. This is still a business trip.

I'm returning with that mindset. It's no different from any other road game. We'll be dialed in and ready to go.

That was the drive of the game and featured many missed opportunities. It was the first drive we watched Monday as a full defense.

The focus was what we failed to execute to get off the field. Sometimes they made a good call against the defense we were playing, and they were going to gain a few yards. But on several plays, it was us. We have to execute in those moments and not try to do too much.

It wasn't from a lack of trying, desire, effort or strain. It was about straining with the necessary focus. If we execute what our jobs ask us to do, many of those assignments weren't complex.

That's where we need to grow. We have to understand formations. By that point in the game, when they enter a certain formation, you should know what play is coming and anticipate it. Every snap shouldn't feel like a new play.

That's part of the process and where we need to improve.

After the South Carolina game, we changed how I address the players at halftime, beginning with the Texas week. We've altered that process, and I think it has helped. We'll continue doing it.

There's nothing magical about it beyond being dialed in and understanding the importance of that moment. Whenever you take the field, the first drive of the second half is as important as the first drive of the game.

We usually watch around 10 to 20 plays as a full unit because there's limited meeting time. You want the entire defense to hear more than its individual corrections and understand how the whole defense fits together.

If you try to correct every play from an entire game during one meeting, it takes multiple hours. We don't have that time. I usually select early drives, if not the first one or two.

That drive was so crucial that everybody needed to understand how a possession reaches 20 plays. It can be the play call, execution or the opponent making a good play. Then, everything begins stacking.

One guy says, "That was my fault on that play." Then, another player says the same thing about the next play. Eventually, everybody raises his hand and admits he had a mistake on the drive. That's how a possession reaches 20 plays.

An eight-play drive is as excruciating as a 20-play drive. They're all difficult.

I was part of a 24-play drive against Missouri in 2020 that ended without points because of a fourth-down stop. The players were so exhausted by the end that they couldn't celebrate. You were trying to excite them because they allowed no points, but they only wanted the bench.

That's the other piece. There's no punter you can call upon while you're on defense. If you want to leave the field, you have to earn your way off it. The only kicker who can enter belongs to the other team after it scores.

We understand the assignment, and we have to do better on third down. We had played solidly during the second half to that point and had opportunities.

Two plays from the drive really stand out. We can't jump offside on third-and-6 coming out of a timeout. Before that, Joseph Mbatchou made a great play to create a loss on first down. On second down, we had an opportunity to record a sack and create third-and-17 or third-and-18, but we didn't get the quarterback down.

Instead, they reached another third down and converted. It should have been third-and-extra-long, which would have made things interesting.

It was a mixture of things. Sometimes, you would like the corners to use more tempo, but everything can't be press-man coverage. You have to play off at times, read through the three-step drop and play with tempo.

We can play faster in certain situations and will continue building in that area. It's easy for a casual observer to say, "Slow down and allow him to catch it." But if the receiver runs past the corner and catches a deep ball, people ask why the defender didn't stay on his upfield shoulder.

When a receiver releases with great pace, he stresses the corner. The defender pedals with more pace than he might want, the receiver breaks outside and the quarterback delivers on time. Sometimes, that throw is the offense's access built into the play.

You hope the pressure affects the quarterback so he can't see it. Sometimes, you press-bail so he doesn't immediately think the throw is available. There are various reasons for it.

On the third down near the end, the defense checked to zone when it should have remained in man. It was a gray area, and I'll take responsibility. I should have hard-called man coverage.

Earlier on third-and-medium, I hard-called man, and they ran mesh, which is a man-beater. You can't chase it down before they throw underneath the pick, and they converted.

Later, we allowed the defense to check to zone if the offense condensed its formation so we could pass the routes. It entered a gray area, and the players checked to zone when we wanted to remain in man. I'll take responsibility for that.

It was really close. Sometimes, the opponent makes a good throw and catch.

The coaching point is that he had Kofi Asare inside for body presence, so he didn't need to play the slant so heavily in that coverage. We were trying to help him so he could defend the fade and deeper route.

Coming out of the break, if he keeps his eyes on the receiver for one more step — we always say two steps to the man — he might make the play. Ultimately, it was bang-bang. Those are the minute details you try to coach. The technique won't always be perfect during a game, although the alignment and communication should be perfect.

There will always be coaching points within the technique.

Everybody needs encouragement at times, regardless of the level. Whether you're a defensive lineman, linebacker or cornerback exposed on the outside, you need somebody to pick you up after a bad play.

I thought he did a good job handling it. He played all 20 snaps of that drive, which wears on a player as the offense moves downfield. That's the cumulative effect of a 20-play drive and why you have to get yourself off the field.

He continues to progress after taking some lumps early.

Like many young players, he had to learn how to grow through those experiences, gain confidence from the good plays and learn from the bad ones. He's beginning to do that.

This is obviously a significant year of growth for him, and the offseason will be important. He still needs to become denser and stronger, particularly in the running game. That will help him set edges against larger receivers and tight ends and become firmer at the top of route stems.

He'll have a lot of tape he can use to build confidence, but also plenty showing where he must improve.

He's playing the same position and role, but he's performing at a high level. You feel him wherever the ball goes. Myles is going to be there. We're pleased with his play and can feel his presence. He has taken on a more vocal role, which we've encouraged. We're going to continue leaning on him during the final stretch, and we need him to keep playing at a high level.

Probably. I would have to review the entire season. But during the past couple of games, his production has been unequivocal.

He's probably slightly ahead of where many true sophomores would be. In his mind, and probably ours, we might have expected more pass-rush production at this point.

He has been unlucky a few times. Against Georgia, he was held on consecutive plays. One was called, and one wasn't. Those could have become sacks that won't appear in the statistics. He also came close to another one and forced Mateer to throw the ball away on a third down during the second half.

He's close. The consistency of his pass-rush plan and knowing which move to use are still developing. His rush lines have improved throughout the season. Now, he has to understand what to use in each moment without pressing.

A home-run hitter who hasn't homered recently might swing harder, but that doesn't mean the ball will travel farther. A golfer who swings harder might only hit the ball farther left or right. A smoother swing produces more distance.

We tell him to remain true to himself, his rushes and the game plan. The production will come. Once the floodgates open, I think they'll really open. We need one of those games like Auburn, when we thought it might begin.

He hasn't been underwhelming or disappointing. You feel his presence in the running and passing games. He has affected quarterbacks even when the statistical production hasn't followed.

He's beginning to recognize that he can do more than provide an interior presence. He can move, take stunt steps, affect the quarterback and pass rush.

Those steps and small confidence-builders are what the defense needs as a whole. One player gains confidence here, another does it there, and they begin trusting themselves and the teammates around them.

That's why they're playing more confidently as a unit. We're nowhere near where we need to be, and the execution isn't close to where it must become. But the effort, confidence and ability to play at a higher level have increased during the past several weeks.

#2678. Pio Esposito shrugs off penalty ghosts as he continues impressive scoring streak for Italy

MILAN (AP) — Having been touted as Italy's next great center forward, Pio Esposito is certainly living up to his promise.

Esposito scored two goals in a commanding performance on Thursday as Italy beat France 3-1 in the Nations League for a first victory over Les Bleus on home soil in 64 years.

The 21-year-old forward took his tally to nine goals for Italy in just 14 matches and also went some way toward expelling the memories from Italy's World Cup playoff defeat to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Esposito's second goal on Thursday came from the penalty spot, sealing the 3-1 result in the 75th minute. It was the first spot kick he had taken since missing one in a penalty shootout defeat to Bosnia that saw the Azzurri fail to qualify for a third straight World Cup.

"When I stepped up to the penalty spot, that memory came back to me — but I couldn't hide for the rest of my life. You have to summon the courage to take them," Esposito said.

There was also an extra weight to the penalty: Pio's older brother, Sebastiano, had missed a spot kick 15 minutes earlier, when the score was still 1-1.

"There was also an added responsibility: to make people forget my brother's mistake," Pio said. "When he made that mistake, it was tough for me, too, and I had to seal the result for his sake as well."

Italy coach Roberto Mancini had seemed as surprised as most at San Siro when Sebastiano stepped up to take the earlier penalty, which he blazed wide. And Mancini confirmed after the match that Pio was top of the penalty takers' list, with Sebastiano second.

"It was a family thing," Mancini added with a smile.

In fact, when Italy got the second spot kick, Mancini turned to Sebastiano — who had been substituted off — on the Azzurri bench and jokingly asked if he wanted to take that one, too. Both laughed.

It has been a remarkable rise for Pio Esposito, who was playing in Serie B — on loan at Spezia — until the start of last season, before a breakout campaign back at Inter Milan.

The youngster was given a standing ovation on Thursday by the crowd of nearly 71,500 at San Siro when he was substituted off in stoppage time.

Pio Esposito could finally be the forward who takes over Gigi Riva's crown as Italy's all-time record scorer with 35 goals — a mark that has stood for 52 years.

"We hope he can score a lot more, because it's been a lifetime that Gigi Riva is at the top," Mancini said. "We hope someone surpasses him for the good of the national team.

"Certainly Pio has a great score at the moment, compared to the matches played."

Next up for Italy is an away match against Belgium, when the Azzurri can seal their place in the quarterfinals as group winners.

Italy lost at home to Belgium in Mancini's first match back in charge. But it has appeared a team transformed since then.

"I am happy that I and we are doing well," Pio said.

#2676. MLB free agency: Predicting landing spots for top players, including Jazz Chisholm Jr., Freddy Peralta, more

Free agency is officially open. As of Monday, five days after the Milwaukee Brewers clinched the first World Series title in franchise history, eligible players are able to talk to and negotiate with all 30 teams with the hopes of finding their new employer. Some will get long-term deals worth more than most of us could ever dream of.

So who goes where? That's for agents and general managers to figure out. We already covered Tarik Skubal, so your CBS Sports experts are digging a bit deeper down the list for a new round of guessing games.

Mike Axisa: There are already rumblings that Morejon wants to start in 2027 and I reckon more than a few teams will be willing to give him that opportunity. The Cubs need all kinds of pitching, both starters and relievers, and can make it work even if Morejon can't hack it as a starter and needs to return to the bullpen. Regardless of role, he's an excellent pitcher, and few teams need as much pitching as the Cubs this winter. It's a perfect match.

Dayn Perry: Any team can use a lockdown reliever like Morejon, who's also young for a free agent. He's got the repertoire to be a starter conversion, too. The Yankees could use him, of course, and I expect they'll pay what it takes.

Matt Snyder: The Cubs badly need rotation help and Wrigley Field, thanks to Chicago wind patterns, is better suited for left-handed pitchers. The ownership there spends money, yes, but is relatively cheap given their market and money-making ability, which means they'll cheap out on Tarik Skubal (if they even try seriously, and my guess is they won't). So they'll need consolation prizes (yes, plural). Morejon will convert to starting and be one of them.

Mike Axisa: Rogers is underrated and he'll have an awful lot of suitors among teams that rely heavily on analytical models this offseason. He has four pitches that grade out as above average, plus he's already demonstrated the ability to get chase out of the zone and limit weak contact. It feels like he's a tweak or two away from becoming a frontline starter, or very close to one. The Mets match up well. They're data-heavy and they need a starting pitcher.

Dayn Perry: Even with some injured arms in line to return at various points in 2027, the Cubs still need rotation help, especially since they share a division with the champion Brewers. I can't see the Ricketts family, who doesn't spend nearly as much it should given the deep coffers the Cubs have, paying for Tarik Skubal. So Rogers it is, since he's arguably the second-best rotation arm on the market.

Matt Snyder: The Braves were hit with a litany of pitching injuries last season and still won the division, but there are a ton of question marks here. Spencer Strider and Spencer Schwellenbach are on that list for sure, but what about Chris Sale? He's heading toward his age-37 year and there's a club option for 2028 before he hits free agency. Grabbing Rogers here provides immediate help, depth and -- assuming it's a long-term deal -- an option to take over as the top lefty once Sale is out.

Mike Axisa: The Cubs have long been rumored as a landing spot for Peralta because of the Craig Counsell connection, though I like the other Chicago team as a fit better. The White Sox are on the rise and they badly need starting pitching. Openers and bullpen games work great in moderation. When you're doing it three or four times each turn through the rotation, it's too much. Peralta will take the ball every five days like clockwork and he's a pretty darn good pitcher too. The ChiSox need both the reliability and upside.

Dayn Perry: Yeah, I'm going with the upset here. Peralta improved significantly under the Rays' watch after the deadline deal that brought him there from the Mets, which means this tracks as a mutually beneficial relationship. With a new ballpark all but assured and a forthcoming CBA that should benefit smaller markets -- and with Stu Sternberg no longer in charge -- the Rays may be poised to actually spend a little.

Matt Snyder: We know that Jerry Dipoto doesn't like to sit still and after the Mariners came within one win of their first World Series, they were bad in 2026. They are still built to win now, especially in an awful division, but they'll reshape the team. I could see trades of starters Logan Gilbert and/or George Kirby that create the need for a rotation replacement in free agency, and Peralta would surely love pitching in that ballpark.

Mike Axisa: Ernie Clement crashed hard in the second half and has always fit better as a super utility guy who moves around rather than someone who plays one set position every day. The Blue Jays desperately need a power infusion, particularly from the left side of the plate, and Chisholm's defense and baserunning will fit in nicely as well. I wonder if any teams would show interest in Chisholm at third base or center field, two positions he's played in the past. Second base in Toronto is my best guess for now.

Dayn Perry: Detroit had pretty good luck with another outgoing Yankees second baseman (Gleyber Torres), so why not another? Dayn Perry: Arozarena is coming off an excellent season with Seattle, and the Phillies, still trying to make the most of their closing window, badly need an upgrade at the outfield corners. Philly hasn't been shy about investing in the on-field product, which means adding the likes of Arozarena would be fully in character.

Matt Snyder: The Phillies' window of contention remains open, even if not for long, and team president Dave Dombrowski isn't shy about adding short-term fixes to his roster. Adolis Garcia didn't work out last year, but that doesn't mean Dombrowski will be shy this time around. They still want to win a World Series with this nucleus and they need corner outfield help, among other things.

#2675. Bengals activate three players off the IR. Here's what it means

The Cincinnati Bengals had three familiar faces return to practice ahead of their primetime showdown with the Pittsburgh Steelers.

The Bengals on Nov. 12 activated three players − receiver Andrei Iosivas, cornerback Jalen Davis and guard Brian Parker II − from the reserve/injured list.

Iosivas injured his thumb, which later required surgery, during a play on special teams during Cincinnati's Week 2 victory against the Houston Texans.

Davis was placed on the IR Sept. 29 with a hamstring injury, and Parker returned after months away due to a knee injury that landed him on the IR Aug. 30.

The players' respective returns to practice commenced a 21-day period where their presence won't count against the team's 53-man roster.

The Bengals on Nov. 15 host the Steelers at Paycor Stadium on Sunday Night Football with a scheduled 8:20 p.m. kickoff.

#2674. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2673. Serbia vs. Germany preview: Team news and predicted lineups

Germany will be looking to put themselves in the strongest possible position ahead of a potential Group A2 decider against the Netherlands next week when they travel to Belgrade to face Serbia on Friday at 20:45 in their penultimate 2026/27 UEFA Nations League group-stage fixture.

The two teams met last month, with Germany taking a 2-0 win at home thanks to goals from Tom Bischof and Florian Wirtz.

That victory remains Germany's only win under Jürgen Klopp, with Die Nationalmannschaft currently sitting third in Group A2 on five points, behind the Netherlands and Greece on eight points and ahead of bottom-placed Serbia, who have yet to pick up a point.

Last month, Serbia were ordered to play the upcoming game against Germany behind closed doors after their fans engaged in racist and discriminatory behaviour during matches against Greece and the Netherlands.

However, Friday's game at the Rajko Mitić Stadium in Belgrade will not be played entirely without spectators.

As the Serbian Football Association confirmed to DPA upon request, a clause in UEFA regulations will allow children under the age of 15 to attend the match, provided they are accompanied by teachers or coaches, with around 5,000 expected to be in attendance.

After calling up a total of 44 players for his first four games as Germany coach, Klopp has named a more streamlined 24-man squad this time around. Borussia Mönchengladbach's Wael Mohya, VfB Stuttgart's Finn Jeltsch and RB Leipzig's Brajan Gruda could potentially make their Germany debuts.

Klopp also notably opted to bring Werder Bremen's Niclas Füllkrug back into the squad, with the West Ham loanee currently topping the Bundesliga scoring charts with nine league goals.

Saša Lukić and Nemanja Maksimović are both suspended for Serbia, while Aleksandar Stanković, Andrej Ilić, Strahinja Pavlović and Adem Avdić are set to miss out through injury.

Germany, meanwhile, will be without Jamal Musiala, Serge Gnabry, Waldemar Anton, Assan Ouédraogo and Angelo Stiller due to injuries.

Said El Mala sat out Germany's training session on Tuesday, but his absence is likely to have been part of a workload-management programme, with the 1. FC Köln star is expected to be fit for the match.

#2672. How busy will the MLB offseason be before likely lockout? Insiders weigh in on November's urgency, uncertainty

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Hot stove season is underway in Major League Baseball. And with a lockout looming when the current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, the next four weeks will likely be the only time that teams have to sign free agents, make trades and reshape their rosters before transactions come to a halt.

Want some context into just how much of a mad dash this could become? One brief exchange with a head of baseball operations offered a glimpse. When asked what his club anticipated in the coming weeks, the executive offered only this: "I'm going to stiff arm you on this one," the exec said. "Because I'm time constrained right now. A lot going on with staff and player conversations."

Urgency will play a role this November. Naturally, teams don't want to be left behind. And the way modern baseball conducts business could be challenged.

Over the last five years, the early stages of MLB's offseason have been largely anticlimactic. Front offices, many of which rely on similar analytical models, have increasingly approached the market with caution, contributing to a process that can drag well into the winter.

Even the Winter Meetings, traditionally a gathering place in early December for blockbuster trades and significant free-agent signings, have increasingly become more of a launching pad for offseason conversations than a destination for completed deals.

So, what does this peculiar November have in store? Yes, there will be moves. But according to one high-ranking league executive, don't expect the approaches that have defined the modern offseason to change entirely. The urgency might be different, but the process of gathering information, evaluating talent and understanding the market remains largely the same.

"You can't get caught flat-footed, so we're going through the same motions of lining up who we like, identifying different ways to meet our needs, calling agents and letting them know we have interest," the executive said. "Next week at GM meetings will be helpful to learn more. That's usually when we indicate we want to zoom with a player and we'll see how agents/players react to that."

Trades, certainly, could take precedence over free-agent signings, given the circumstances and the talent available. This year's free-agent class is notably weak, particularly when it comes to starting pitching. The trade market, meanwhile, could offer alternatives that free agency simply doesn't.

One left-handed starter from the Los Angeles Angels, who isn't set to become a free agent until 2029, figures to be particularly coveted.

"A bunch of teams need pitching based on our initial sweepstakes," the executive continued. "So I think names like Reid Detmers will be in high demand. If you're a team in on him, it might be worth overpaying to jump the line. After [Tarik] Skubal, none of the starting pitching free agent names are that exciting."

No team wants to get left behind. But with the uncertainty surrounding 2027 and little indication of what next year might look like, teams don't want to overreact, either. The temptation to move quickly must be weighed against the consequences of making the wrong move.

Reacting to an opponent's moves, as that same executive suggested, can prove costly. Particularly in a market where the pressure to act could drive up the price of acquiring talent.

More importantly, all of this remains a moving target. The uncertainty surrounding the next season complicates even the most straightforward roster decisions. Rentals, as one front-office official put it, aren't particularly attractive given the circumstances. In the (still seemingly unlikely) event that there's no baseball in 2027, trading away prospects or valuable big-league talent for a player with only one year of control becomes a considerable gamble. A team could surrender valuable assets without ever getting the opportunity to benefit from the acquisition.

Years of contractual control carry even greater value now. Teams recognize that, which could ultimately stall trades. The very players who might offer the most security in an uncertain market could also become the most difficult to acquire.

"We're really operating under uncertainty now," one front-office person said.

Now, that isn't to suggest free-agent deals won't get done. In fact, one agent said he wouldn't be surprised to see a flurry of mid-tier players reach agreements ahead of the Dec. 1 CBA expiration, pointing to the activity leading up to the 2021–22 lockout as evidence of how an approaching deadline can accelerate an otherwise slow-moving market.

"Last time there was going to be a lockout it was extremely active for Kevin Gausman and Marcus Stroman, who were free agents entering 2022," the agent said.

Gausman signed a five-year, $110 million deal with the Toronto Blue Jays, while Stroman inked a three-year, $71 million contract with the Chicago Cubs. Corey Seager and Marcus Semien, meanwhile, agreed to huge deals with the Texas Rangers. A total of $1.7 billion in free-agent contracts were agreed to prior to the lockout.

This year, Sonny Gray, Tyler Mahle, and Gausman, again, certainly fit that second-tier group.

"Nothing motivates clubs more than a deadline, so I'd be shocked if there wasn't a flurry of deals prior to the deadline," the agent said.

Whether through trades or free agency, the expectation remains that deals will get done in the next four weeks. It will be a fascinating November.

The Bengals on Nov. 12 activated three players − receiver Andrei Iosivas, cornerback Jalen Davis and guard Brian Parker II − from the reserve/injured list.

Iosivas injured his thumb, which later required surgery, during a play on special teams during Cincinnati's Week 2 victory against the Houston Texans.

Davis was placed on the IR Sept. 29 with a hamstring injury, and Parker returned after months away due to a knee injury that landed him on the IR Aug. 30.

The players' respective returns to practice commenced a 21-day period where their presence won't count against the team's 53-man roster.

The Bengals on Nov. 15 host the Steelers at Paycor Stadium on Sunday Night Football with a scheduled 8:20 p.m. kickoff.

#2669. Brewers' Pat Murphy apologized to Yankees' Brian Cashman over viral comment about Jake Bauers free agency

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the aftermath of the World Series championship, Brewers manager Pat Murphy was caught on a hot mic talking to first baseman and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, who heads into free agency this winter off a career year.

Murphy's message? "You're gonna be a rich f---er, but just remember when you were on that horseshit Yankees team and you guys were all playing for yourself, just remember, say, 'this is the way we used to do it.'"

The comment, predictably, drew backlash from those who assumed Murphy was taking a shot at the Yankees. Bauers was on the 2023 Yankees, when they went 82-80 and missed the playoffs.

"I called Brian Cashman right away when I heard it got out," Murphy said on the New York Post's "The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman released on Tuesday. "I picked up a phone and called Brian right away, and had a good conversation. And the best I could try to explain that I wasn't talking about the 2026 Yankees.

"After every celebration, I'd shake his hand. I'd say, 'You rich so-and-so, you're going to leave us,' " Murphy explained. "We're not going to be able to pay you. You're going to leave us and you're going to forget all about how we did things. … I would just give him this rhetoric every time.

"I was just referring to the teams that have a lot of high-paid, long-contract players," Murphy said. "That sometimes it's harder to get all those guys together to play together. And I used the Yankees because I knew Jake was with them before. … I regret saying it, but that was Jake and I's humor behind the scenes and I got caught."

First off, dudes talking to dudes when they don't realize anyone else is listening lends itself to a lot of comments they don't necessarily mean or, perhaps more importantly, don't include the context of a longstanding relationship between a manager and his player. There isn't anything really out of line here in terms of the Yankees shot. Any Yankees fan would tell you they agree with Murphy's assessment of that team.

Where I do believe there's a problem is the insinuation that a player getting a huge payday means that he'll just start playing only for himself instead of doing things as a team. The Dodgers' high individual salaries certainly didn't stop them from winning two straight World Series titles.

Further, Bauers made $2.7 million last season, double his previous high. MLB players have a finite shelf life and need the money they make to stretch, if they're lucky, for generations. He's set to make exponentially more in free agency in his one big payday to hopefully set up his family for decades. Some might think it insensitive of Murphy to mock that a player might need to look out for himself and his family.

Then again, take note of Murphy's quote when he says that's just their sense of humor. We don't know their personal relationship because it is just that: personal. Unless Bauers signs elsewhere and comes out guns blazing against Murphy, this whole thing is probably just much ado about nothing. It would be pretty shocking if Cashman took particular offense, either.

#2666. ‘He’s Got To Do All 500’: Ryan Preece Going Through With Crazy Chris Buescher Bet

RFK Racing teammates Chris Buescher and Ryan Preece made a bet with each other at the beginning of the Chase. Between the two of them, whoever finishes lower than the other in the 2026 NASCAR Cup Series points standings has to drive 500 laps around a roundabout.

Preece finished 15th in the final standings, while Buescher ranked 14 points behind him in 16th place.

A bet is a bet, and now Buescher is the one that has to pay up.

Preece is not letting Buescher off the hook after finishing behind him in the final Cup Series standings.

"I'm not going to be the guy driving around the roundabout 500 times," Preece said.

When asked about the bet during NASCAR Awards media availability on Tuesday night, Preece said he will have a front-row seat as his teammate complete 500 laps around a roundabout.

"I'm going to be sitting in the center of that roundabout with a camera," Preece said.

Of course, doing 500 laps around a roundabout on a public roadway comes with the threat of getting in trouble. NASCAR reporter Andrew Kurland suggested if Preece would call it an "official race" if Buescher made it past 250 laps, then got pulled over by police.

The reference was to NASCAR's inclement weather procedure, where a race can be called official due to precipitation if the race is past the halfway mark.

Preece was adamant, however, that no such thing will happen. Buescher must complete the 500 laps as part of the bet.

"Oh no, he's got to do all 500 [laps]. I'm getting a transponder and I'm going to register a race monitor somehow," Preece said.

Perhaps Preece could get help from a friend of his who is a police officer and scout out the perfect roundabout for Buescher to fulfill the bet.

"I'm probably going to go scope out some spots. Maybe talk to a friend of mine that's a cop to see if … what the best time [is]," Preece said.

Preece said he is not sure if they will paint up Buescher's vehicle like a race car for the 500-lap roundabout bet but is open to ideas from the fans.

"That's a good idea. I don't know. … We're open to suggestions from the fans," Preece said.

In more serious matters for RFK Racing, Brad Keselowski just wrapped up his fifth and final season as driver and car owner of the organization. While Keselowski's racing future is unclear, the former driver of the No. 6 said he has six different options for 2027.

Preece will transition from the No. 60 to the No. 6 beginning in 2027, keeping one of Roush's most historic numbers on the racetrack. Buescher will remain the driver of the No. 17 as a two-car operation next year.

The ownership of RFK Racing is unclear, in terms of whether the organization will keep the name or revert back to Roush Fenway Racing.

In 2026, Preece scored RFK Racing's only win, which was the regular-season finale race at Daytona. It marked Preece's first points-paying win and locked him into the 2026 Chase. Preece also won the Cook Out Clash exhibition race at Bowman-Gray Stadium to open the 2026 season.

Former Major League Baseball star Mark Teixeira is headed to Capitol Hill after winning the election for the United States House of Representatives seat in Texas' 21st district on Tuesday. Teixeira, the Republican candidate, beat Democrat Kristin Hook, a former federal scientist.

Teixeira will now take over the seat vacated by Republican Chip Roy, who didn't seek re-election.

"Together, we can build a better future for our families, our neighbors, and every community across Texas 21," Teixeira said in a statement. "I'm excited to get to work. I will be praying for all of you and for the future of this great nation. God bless Texas, and God bless America."

He was a rare win for the GOP in Texas on Tuesday, as Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the gubernatorial race and Democrat James Talarico flipped the Senate seat.

Teixeira, 46, was born and raised in Maryland before attending Georgia Tech as a big-time prospect. He was selected fifth overall in the first round of the 2001 Draft by the Rangers. He then came up through the Rangers' system and spent the first four and a half seasons of his career with the ballclub. He was traded to the Braves in 2007, then to the Angels in 2008 before signing a long-term free agent deal with the Yankees prior to the 2009 season. He finished his career with the Yankees.

In parts of 14 seasons, Teixeira hit .268/.360/.509 (126 OPS+) with 409 home runs, 1,298 RBI, five Gold Gloves, three All-Star Games, three Silver Sluggers and a World Series ring.

Teixeira is one of several familiar sports faces up for election on Tuesday. Former college football coach Tommy Tuberville won the Alabama gubernatorial race and former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya lost the Minnesota Senate race.

Golden State Warriors big man Kristaps Porzingis announced Friday that he has "made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love" as he continues to deal with mysterious health issues. It's unclear when, or if, the 31-year-old Porziņģis will return to the court.

Porziņģis has not played for the Warriors this season and reports earlier this week indicated that the team is withholding payments from him. He signed a two-year, $40 million deal with the Warriors in free agency this summer, but the second year of the deal only has a $3 million guarantee.

Here is Porziņģis' full statement announcing his decision to step away from basketball:

This season I was really looking forward to running it with this group, but as I ramped up, my body didn't respond the way I anticipated.

I'm doing good, but I know what it takes, and I'm not where I want to be to perform at the level that I expect from myself. At this point, I've made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love.

In this situation, I want to show the utmost respect for the Golden State Warriors and work with them to find a solution that makes sense.

I'm thankful to my family and close ones for always being there. Much appreciation to all of you for the support.

Porziņģis' career has been defined by health problems. He's played more than 57 games just three times since he was drafted No. 4 overall by the New York Knicks in 2015, and has dealt with significant injuries, including a torn ACL that cost him the entire 2018-19 season. In recent years, he's been limited by this mysterious illness that first became an issue in Boston during the 2024-25 season.

Porziņģis started dealing with extreme fatigue and previously disclosed a diagnosis of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS, which is characterized by rapid changes in heart rate when a person stands up and can lead to exhaustion and dizziness.

"You know how people say, 'Oh, I'm so fatigued.' I've never used those words. I don't even like to speak in those terms, but I really was like that," Porziņģis said ahead of last season. "At that time, I could just lay on the couch and be a house cat."

Over the last three seasons with the Celtics, Atlanta Hawks and Warriors, Porziņģis has only played 74 games. He has been away from the Warriors since late September and released a previous statement in mid-October shutting down rumors that he had been diagnosed with HIV or AIDS. At that point, the Warriors said Porziņģis would be out indefinitely.

"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap. Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon," Porziņģis wrote. "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support."

The Warriors hoped that Porziņģis would play a big role this season as a floor-spacing big, especially while Jimmy Butler (torn ACL) and Moses Moody (torn patellar tendon) remain sidelined. Instead, it seems more likely that he will never play for the franchise again.

The Warriors have reportedly been trying to trade Porziņģis to use his $20 million cap figure, as explained by CBS Sports' Sam Quinn:

While he would not have trade value as a player given his health status, he is essentially an expiring contract with only that small $3 million guarantee on the books for next season. That could potentially make him valuable to a team looking to move off of longer-term money, or the Warriors could entice another team into a trade using draft picks with Porziņģis serving only as the matching salary.

Despite Porziņģis' absence, the Warriors are off to a 6-3 start, putting them in seventh place in the extremely crowded Western Conference standings. Rookie big man Yaxel Lendeborg has stepped up in Porziņģis' place and provided a major boost on both ends of the floor.

Through nine games, Lendeborg is averaging 21 points, 7.1 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 1.1 steals while shooting 49.2% from the field, including 39.6% from 3-point range.

However, Bild head of football Christian Falk has now played down the speculation, suggesting that the 27-year-old is "too old and far too good" for a move to the German champions to be a realistic option.

“He’s now too old and far too good for it to be an option for FC Bayern – especially at a time when the club is already fully stocked in this position,” Falk said in quotes published on his CfBayern Insider website.

The German journalist added that Bayern did show genuine interest in Ødegaard when he was still young and making his way through the ranks.

“Remember, when he was very, very young (I think about 16 or so), he was at Säbener Straße for a training session week when Pep Guardiola was the manager. At this point, it was very interesting for FC Bayern to sign the player, but they didn’t get him in the end," he said, before adding:

“It’s always nice to see such names connected with the Bundesliga giants, but he won’t be coming to Bayern any time soon.”

#2659. MLB rumors: The only Oriole not on the trading block, Rays' Drew Rasmussen plan and Astros add to manager hunt

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Brewers have now been World Series champions for just one week (minus a few hours) and they should still be basking in the glory for quite a while. As the offseason marches on, the next big date will be Nov. 17, when decisions on qualifying offers are due from the eight players who received one.

In the meantime, the rumor mill should be ever-so-slowly churning. We'll round it up here.

The Houston Astros moved on from general manager Dana Brown in August and fired manager Joe Espada after the 2026 season. Newly hired general manager Randy Flores is now tasked with landing a new dugout boss, and a three-time MVP and future Hall of Famer is in the mix. The Astros will interview Albert Pujols for the manager job this week, per The Athletic.

Pujols has long made it known that he desires to be an MLB manager. He recently interviewed for vacancies with the Padres and Angels (both last offseason) and he also managed the Dominican Republic in the World Baseball Classic this past spring. It should be further noted that Pujols is in the fourth year of a 10-year, $100 personal services contract with the Angels that was part of the mega-deal he signed with them as a player prior to the 2012 season as a player.

Other known candidates for the Astros manager job are Rangers bench coach Luis Urueta and Yankees bench coach (not to mention former Tigers and Angels manager) Brad Ausmus. Former Astros third baseman Morgan Ensberg, the manager of the Triple-A Rays affiliate Durham Bulls, will also interview this week, according to MLB.com.

The Orioles are willing to listen to trade offers on any player other than Pete Alonso as they seek both rotation and outfield help, according to The Baltimore Banner. The  Orioles reportedly aren't "actively shopping" any players, but they are looking for upgrades at starting pitcher and outfielder and realize one of the ways that could happen is via a trade.

Surely they wouldn't sell low on Gunnar Henderson, given his immense upside, so we can probably take him off the table unless some team makes it worth their while. There is a glut of infielders, though. With Alonso at first base and Henderson at short, they have Jackson Holliday, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, Jordan Westburg and Coby Mayo for two spots. Even using one of the four at designated hitter, it's easy to see where a deal could happen.

Westburg and Encarnacion-Strand are under team control through 2029 while Holliday is controlled through 2030 and Mayo through 2031.

The American League champion Rays recently picked up the $20 million club option on All-Star starting pitcher Drew Rasmussen. That would be a franchise-record salary for one player in a single season. It might seem odd to exercise an option and then deal a player to an outsider, but locking Rasmussen in for a one-year deal makes him an attractive trade candidate instead of just letting him walk in free agency, and this is how the Rays generally operate. We've seen it so many times: they get ahead of losing guys to free agency, sometimes even dealing them a year or two earlier. They've done it with Randy Arozarena, Isaac Paredes, Tyler Glasnow and even going back to franchise legends like David Price, Evan Longoria and Ben Zobrist.

The Rays right now are saying they intend to keep Rasmussen for 2027.

"Not a declarative this, that, whatever, but I can sit here very confidently and say that every intention right now is thinking about Ras anchoring our rotation and how to make this team better going into next year," club president Erik Neander said on Tuesday, via the Tampa Bay Times.

If they want to contend again next year, it sure seems like they need Rasmussen, with Nick Martinez and Freddy Peralta off to free agency. That leaves Rasmussen atop the rotation, followed by Shane McClanahan, Griffin Jax, Ryan Pepiot and a bunch of question marks. There are questions attached to McClanahan, Jax and Pepiot too.

#2657. TCU is working to add former Saint Louis player Robbie Avila after return to Billikens was nixed

FORT WORTH, Texas (AP) — TCU is working to add Robbie Avila to its roster after the former Saint Louis player was cleared to play by a judge but barred from returning to the Billikens due to roster restrictions.

Horned Frogs coach Jamie Dixon said Thursday he was contacted by Avila and his family after the fifth-year senior exhausted "all options to play at Saint Louis" and became aware of the injury situation at TCU. The Horned Frogs are without Texas Tech transfer Luke Bamgboye indefinitely.

Dixon said he had informed the team that the school was in the process of finalizing the eligibility of Avila, the reigning Atlantic 10 player of the year who became a sensation for his signature specs at Indiana State.

Avila was granted a fifth year under preliminary injunction, but the College Sports Commission ruled he couldn't play for Saint Louis due to the roster restrictions.

It was unlikely that Avila would be available for the Horned Frogs against Milwaukee on Friday night. Their next game is at home against Texas A&M on Nov. 19.

The Billikens won a school-record 29 games last season behind Avila, reaching the second round of the NCAA Tournament before losing to eventual national champion Michigan.

He averaged 12.8 points and 4.5 rebounds last season and has career averages of 14.5 points and 5.5 rebounds over four seasons — two each with Indiana State and Saint Louis.

The Horned Frogs are 3-0 but needed double overtime for a 100-92 victory over UL Monroe at home on Tuesday.

#2656. Biggest MLB offseason questions: How long will lockout last? Will we see a free agency frenzy?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Not so long ago, the Milwaukee Brewers were crowned World Series champions, and at the moment of the last out, the 2026-27 Major League offseason began. So let's talk about that.

The winter ahead is one shot through with uncertainty, as labor strife figures to roil the sport and perhaps even compromise the 2027 season. Those matters, vital as they are, won't be the only story, and we'll still have the familiar presences of free agency and trade talk to sustain us.

To set the scene for all that's ahead in advance of the 2027 campaign – good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – we're here to take a look at the five questions that will inform an offseason that's going to be quite unusual and – for good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – probably unforgettable. Let's explore those five queries right now …

The current collective bargaining agreement – or CBA, the accord that governs the working relationship between clubs/owners and players – is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year. At that time, MLB owners are all but certain to lock out the players. That's a labor stoppage, and that means the offseason will be brought to a sudden halt. The lockout, the purpose of which is to preempt a players' strike, will last until a new CBA is agreed to. Agreeing to a new CBA will be no simple matter, and owners and their hireling, commissioner Rob Manfred, are pushing for a cap on team payrolls. The players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, have never shown any willingness to agree to a cap-and-floor system. There are a lot of other issues to iron out, as the CBA is an all-encompassing document, but the fight over a cap will be what drags out the lockout.

The heart of the matter is whether the lockout will last long enough to push back, abbreviate, or – perish the thought – cancel entirely the 2027 season. The latter is the worst-case scenario and is highly unlikely, but it's a possibility, however remote. More of a threat is a 2027 season that doesn't span the usual 162 games.

We have a recent precedent to guide us. The last time the CBA was up for negotiation during the offseason of 2021-22, owners locked out the players for 99 days. That meant a shortened spring training by about two and a half weeks and forced the regular season calendar to be compressed, albeit while still preserving the 162-game docket. As such, we can say that if the lockout lasts beyond the middle of March 2027, then we'll likely lose regular-season games.

For further context, here's a brief history of modern labor stoppages in the sport:

Just two, the 1981 and 1994-95 player strikes, significantly compromised seasons. The 1994-95 stoppage cost us the 1994 World Series, and it took years for the sport to recover from the resulting fan disaffection.

As for the 2027 season, the worst-case scenario may not be the loss of the entire season but rather the loss of 60 games off the regular-season slate. Here's the explanation from our recent Lockout 101 piece:

"… [I]f the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives."

Obviously, the hope is that the lockout doesn't even affect the spring training calendar, let alone cost us a major chunk of the regular season.

As noted, the big fight is over whether or not MLB will have a cap-and-floor structure moving forward, as is the case in the NFL, NBA, and NHL. Owners have tied every single proposal wrinkle to date to the players' acceptance of a cap. However, it remains highly unlikely, at least until further notice, that the union would ever agree to such a thing.

The other major issue is a likely restructuring of the revenue-sharing system. Specifically, the next CBA is highly likely to revise the system so that local broadcast revenues are shared much more evenly. Fortunately, there's already some common ground on this issue, and a reordering of that system would directly address the revenue disparities within MLB that are such a reliable source of consternation – and misinformation – without the grievous labor war that a continued cap push would force upon us.

Otherwise, some other key wrinkles and changes may come out of the wash. That list potentially includes:

This doesn't get into evergreen matters like an increase in the minimum salary, draft bonus pools, the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, and so forth. There's a lot to sort out, to say the least. The expectation is that the next CBA is going to lead to sweeping changes to the sport starting in 2027 and, perhaps by design, growing over time. Even if there's no cap and floor, the economic structure of MLB is almost certain to look very different after this winter.

Overall, this is one of the weakest free agent classes in living memory, but there is elite superstar value to be found at the tip-top with back-to-back (for the moment) American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

Skubal, who turns 30 on Nov. 20, remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and he's going to be paid like it. The expectation is that he'll wind up signing the largest pitcher contract in MLB history and perhaps also fetch the highest-ever annual salary for a pitcher. It's not out of the question that Skubal's next contract could approach or even surpass $400 million in total value. At those rates, the incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers and the free-spending New York Mets are the consensus favorites. The Chicago Cubs are also reportedly heavily interested in Skubal, and surprise bidders are always possible. Other notable free agent names include Freddy Peralta, Michael King, Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trevor Rogers, Adrian Morejon, and Teruaki Sato. Our ranking of the top 50 2026-27 free agents has you covered.

The "when" of all this is more complicated thanks to the upcoming lockout detailed above. Will premium free agents and their representatives rush to find some stability in advance of the stoppage, during which no major-league transactions will be permitted, or will they decide that the long game will be better for their markets? It's possible that the biggest spenders on the team side will look to make moves early, as the barrel of the next CBA figures to be leveled directly at them and their abundant revenues. Or maybe the unknown will have a chilling effect on spending before we arrive at the lockout.

The past is not always prelude, but let's note that we saw a flurry of spending leading up to the lockout of 2021-22. Indeed, in November 2021, MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents prior to the lockout. The Texas Rangers alone guaranteed $500 million to a new middle infield – Corey Seager and Marcus Semien – before the lockout put an end to such things. In all, teams put ink to paper on five nine-figure contracts prior to the 2021-22 lockout.

The comparisons may not entirely hold since this upcoming CBA should bring about a much more drastic re-ordering of the sport than the current expiring CBA did. As such, teams may proceed cautiously given all the uncertainties. Or, as just mentioned, they may seek to get business done before the ways of doing business change entirely. We'll see soon enough. If we do see the dollars start flying before the lockout, then the upcoming Nov. 10-12 general managers meetings in Las Vegas may occasion the groundwork for all those deals.

Will a lackluster free agent class mean more headline-grabbing trades? That may indeed be answered in the affirmative this winter. Yes, the CBA uncertainty will have a bearing on trades, especially those that involve the assumption of major salary obligations, but big trades still figure to be a prominent part of this offseason.

It's of course impossible to know who's going to be dealt ahead of time, but some big names perhaps on the move this winter include Francisco Lindor, Mason Miller, Spencer Strider, Hunter Greene, Otto Lopez, Jeremy Peña, Ketel Marte, Jacob deGrom, and of course others. Paul Skenes? Almost certainly not, but you'll just as certainly hear his name bandied about.

Turning back to last lockout, it was mostly minor trades before the sport shut down. Yes, we'll see big ones this time around, but they may not happen until we have a new CBA in place and the lockout is over.

Let's make time for the losers, shall we? The teams that didn't make the postseason in 2026 and otherwise qualify will take part in the draft lottery, which is presently scheduled for Dec. 8. That lottery will determine which teams get the top six picks in the 2027 MLB Draft.

This year, 16 of the 18 non-playoff teams will be in the lottery. Non-playoff teams can be barred from the lottery if they've had lottery picks in two consecutive seasons. If a team is a revenue-sharing payor, then it can't be in the lottery in consecutive years. Those wrinkles this year mean that the San Francisco Giants and Pittsburgh Pirates will not be in the lottery and can't pick higher than 10th in the 2027 Draft.

Here's how the preliminary lottery odds look for those 16 teams in the mix, based on how they finished the 2026 season:

It's too soon to know which players will be in the mix for that top pick since the amateur seasons haven't begun yet. However, two early favorites to go No. 1 are University of Florida shortstop Brendan Lawson and Mississippi State left-hander Tomas Valinicius.

#2655. The numbers behind Luka Dončić's historic start are entering the realm of ridiculous

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Luka Doncic delivered another casual masterpiece with 53 points in a 124-118 Lakers victory over the Trail Blazers on Friday night. He outscored Portland by himself 20-15 in the third quarter. He dropped a three-quarter-court buzzer-beater to end the first half. He added five rebounds and five assists for fun. And the Lakers are now atop the Western Conference standings at 8-2.

If the season were to end today, Dončić would be the runaway MVP, maybe joining 2015-16 Stephen Curry as the second unanimous winner in NBA history. His box scores will always be somewhat skewed given his usage, but that context notwithstanding, these numbers are downright stupid.

Luka Doncic this season:28 PTS | 8 REB | 7 AST23 PTS | 6 REB | 7 AST52 PTS | 8 REB | 10 AST41 PTS | 5 REB | 9 AST37 PTS | 7 REB | 5 AST45 PTS | 15 REB | 6 AST42 PTS | 7 REB | 13 AST40 PTS | 9 REB | 7 AST53 PTS | 5 REB | 5 ASTMVP? pic.twitter.com/2qjWxSo3E0

Let's dive a little deeper into the numbers behind Dončić's historic start.

Dončić has become the third player in Lakers history to score at least 35 points in seven straight games, joining Kobe Bryant and Elgin Baylor.

Dončić is just the fourth Lakers player to put up four straight 40-point games, joining Bryant, Baylor and George Mikan. You'll notice names like LeBron James, Shaquille O'Neal, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Magic Johnson missing from these lists. Some franchise marks are oversold. Not when it comes to the Lakers.

Dončić has made at least five 3-pointers in seven straight games. If he continues that streak for another five games, he will break James Harden's NBA record of 12 straight.

Dončić is currently averaging six made 3-pointers per game. He has played in nine of the Lakers' 10 games. Meaning, if he stays on this pace of six 3s per game while playing in 90% of L.A.'s games, he would end up making 426 3s, which would break Curry's single-season record of 402.

Staying on six, Dončić also owns the non-Wilt Chamberlain NBA record with six 40-point games in his team's first 10 games.

Dončić has now logged seven straight games with at least 35 points, five assists and five rebounds, tying Oscar Robertson for the longest such streak in history.

Dončić is currently attempting 13.7 3-pointers per game. If that volume holds up, it would break Harden's NBA record of 13.2 attempts per game in 2018-19. But Harden only made 36.8% of his 3s that year. Dončić, as you'll see shortly, is blowing that number out of the water.

LUKA DONCIC FROM 3/4 COURT TO END THE HALF. OMG 🤯 pic.twitter.com/6MZGtF5ahY

With two 50-point games so far and just 11% of the schedule completed, Dončić is currently on pace to cook up 16 50-burgers this season, which would shatter Bryant's non-Chamberlain record of 10 in a single season. Chamberlain, for the record, had 45 50-point games in 1961-62, which is just absurd.

After Friday's performance, Dončić is now averaging 40.1 points per game. The only other player in history to average 40 through the first nine games of a season is Chamberlain, who is basically a category unto himself in these statistical side-by-sides. The most Michael Jordan ever averaged through the first nine games of a season was 38.6 in 1986-87.

Dončić is shooting 41.9% from 3 to start the year. That isn't likely to continue. Like Harden, he's been a volume marksman to this point as a career 35% 3-point shooter. But right now he is absolutely dialed, particularly with his step-back, which, according to NBA.com shot tracking, he entered Friday night knocking down at a Curry-like 43% clip.

Luka made 8 of his first 9 three-point attempts last night against the Raptors. Almost all contested step-backs or pull-ups. Crazy level of shot making... pic.twitter.com/K5GWhxXq2x

Dončić is reading the game on autopilot at this point in his career. If you double him, he's zipping the right pass. If you single cover him, he's either powering his way into the paint or, more often, getting right into this step-back as a matter of routine. And when he's making it, there's nothing any defender in the world can do about it.

The Lakers' 110.2 defensive rating with Dončić on the court would register as a top-10 mark. For all the talk about Dončić's poor defense, he hasn't been nearly as bad with the Lakers as he was with the Mavericks (especially in the 2024 Finals, the clips from which are going to haunt him forever), and he's been downright good so far this season.

It's early, yes, and individual defensive stats can be deceiving, but nonetheless Dončić is tied for sixth league-wide with 15 steals (he's been a genuine ball hawk early), and he's tied for the league lead in charges with four.

And get this: Opponents are shooting just 32.3 percent so far with Dončić as their defender, which is the best mark in the league among all players who are defending at least 12 shots per game. Better than Victor Wembanyama!

Again, these can be deceiving markers. Dončić obviously isn't an elite defender, and that opponent shooting percentage is going to vary wildly on Dončić simply being the closest defender on misses rather than the one genuinely forcing someone into a bad shot. Also, he's defending perimeter shots, so on some level, shooters are just missing a lot of shots with him nearby so far.

But the 3-pointers are the ones where he's just the guy closing out a lot (which is still important). Inside the arc, you're much more responsible for effecting misses, and have a look at this entering the Portland game.

SURPRISE LEADER ON DEFENSE: LUKA DONČIĆOpponents have made only 21.9% of their two-point attempts against Luka Dončić this season. No player in the league has allowed a lower mark among those who have defended at least 30 of them.The top 10:Luka Dončić: 21.9%Miles Bridges:… pic.twitter.com/RCnWEqMHg3

Bottom line, a 110.2 defensive rating with Dončić on the floor is what it is. At the very least, he hasn't been a liability, which, given his offensive production, is a major win.

The Lakers' offensive rating with Dončić on the floor this season, which would be an NBA record. When he isn't on the floor, the offense falls to a 99.1 rating, which would rank as the worst in the league by a long shot. As Austin Reaves is finding out in the non-Luka minutes, life is mighty difficult without one of the greatest offensive players in history out there to command all the attention and still break defenses down like a cardboard box.

Including Friday night, the Lakers have won Dončić's on-floor minutes this season by a total of 140 points and lost his bench minutes by 63.

Do the math, and he has single-handedly represented a 203-point swing so far. If you are looking for one MVP number, this might be it.

#2650. "I might have deserved the opportunity a little more" – Ter Stegen opens up on rivalry with Neuer

Heading into Germany's upcoming games against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen has been named as Jürgen Klopp undisputed first choice in goal.

For the 34-year-old, this marks a welcome change after years of playing second fiddle to Manuel Neuer and struggling with injuries.

In an interview with Sport Bild, ter Stegen looks back on his long-standing rivalry with the now 40-year-old Bayern Munich shot-stopper, who announced his international retirement for good after last summer's World Cup.

While ter Stegen clearly has huge respect for Neuer's qualities, he makes no secret of the fact that he would have liked to play more than the 45 games he has featured in for Germany at senior level.

“Manuel Neuer is not simply a great goalkeeper. We don't need to fool ourselves about that: he is probably one of the best goalkeepers of all time. He also had an enormous standing within the national team, and rightly so. However, he was also held back by injuries,” ter Stegen said.

“And who knows more about that than I do, unfortunately? Nevertheless, I believe a certain level of competition pushes the goalkeeper who gets to play to improve. That's how it was with us.

“Even so, the question naturally remains: would I rather have been playing? Of course! But the coaches we had with the national team chose Manu. You have to respect that, and I have to accept it. That's simply part of sport.”

The 34-year-old did admit that there were times when he felt he deserved to play ahead of Neuer, despite not being given the opportunity.

“Did I sometimes have to bite my tongue? Did I sometimes swear under my breath when nobody was listening? Certainly! There were also moments when I felt I might have deserved the opportunity a little more,” he said.

One particularly bitter moment for ter Stegen came at the 2018 World Cup, when Neuer managed to return from a long-term injury and reclaim his place in the starting line-up ahead of him despite lacking match practice.

“That was the most bitter moment, but I don't want to revisit it. The fact remains that the coach (Jogi Löw at the time, ed.) makes the decision. You can get as angry as you like,” said ter Stegen, who is currently Ajax's first-choice goalkeeper while on loan from FC Barcelona.
